title: Jittery Quantum Boomerang Effect
summary: We study the dynamics of a spin-polarized wave packet in a disordered Rashba two-dimensional electron gas and identify a jittery quantum boomerang effect in which longitudinal and transverse motion return to the origin through fundamentally distinct mechanisms. Starting from an initial state with finite momentum along $x$ and spin polarized along $z$, we calculate the time evolution by combining a Chebyshev expansion of the time-evolution operator with a disorder ensemble average. In the weak-scattering regime, equations of motion derived from the quantum kinetic equation reproduce the numerical trends and show that impurity scattering acts as a viscous damping mechanism that suppresses the transient Zitterbewegung and drives the transverse displacement back to $y=0$ at long times. In contrast, the longitudinal dynamics show a Drude-like saturation at weak disorder. These results are consistent with the vanishing intrinsic spin Hall conductivity in the disordered Rashba model and with experimental observations of a transient intrinsic spin Hall effect in the time-domain. As disorder increases, the longitudinal dynamics evolve to a partial return toward the origin, which signals a transition from weak antilocalization to Anderson localization in 2D.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a jittery quantum boomerang effect in a disordered Rashba 2D electron gas, where longitudinal and transverse motions return to the origin via distinct mechanisms: transverse return is driven by impurity scattering suppressing Zitterbewegung, while longitudinal return shows Drude-like saturation at weak disorder and transitions to Anderson localization at strong disorder.
AI.motivation: To study the dynamics of a spin-polarized wave packet in a disordered Rashba 2D electron gas and identify distinct mechanisms governing longitudinal and transverse quantum boomerang dynamics.
AI.method: Combined Chebyshev expansion of the time-evolution operator with disorder ensemble averaging; quantum kinetic equation-derived equations of motion in the weak-scattering regime.
AI.result: Transverse displacement returns to zero via impurity scattering damping of Zitterbewegung; longitudinal dynamics show Drude-like saturation at weak disorder and partial return signaling a transition from weak antilocalization to Anderson localization as disorder increases.
AI.conclusion: Results are consistent with vanishing intrinsic spin Hall conductivity in the disordered Rashba model and with experimental observations of a transient intrinsic spin Hall effect in the time domain.

title: Magnetic HIP-NN for spin dynamics in disordered itinerant magnets
summary: We present a magnetic extension of the Hierarchically Interacting Particle Neural Network (HIP-NN) that enables large-scale simulations of electron-mediated spin dynamics in disordered itinerant magnets. The resulting magnetic HIP-NN (mHIP-NN) incorporates rotationally invariant spin correlations directly into hierarchical message-passing layers, enabling the network to learn emergent magnetic energy landscapes and effective local fields from coupled geometric-spin environments while preserving spin-rotation symmetry. As a benchmark application, we consider structurally disordered itinerant $s$-$d$ exchange models in which the effective magnetic forces arise dynamically from the instantaneous electronic structure and are computationally prohibitive to evaluate using conventional exact-diagonalization-based approaches. We show that mHIP-NN accurately reproduces the local torques governing Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert dynamics and faithfully captures the nonequilibrium evolution of spatial spin correlations following thermal quenches. Our results establish symmetry-aware hierarchical message-passing networks as an efficient and scalable framework for large-scale simulations of frustrated itinerant spin systems and nonequilibrium magnetic dynamics. More broadly, because the learned energy functional remains fully differentiable with respect to both atomic coordinates and spin variables, the framework also provides a natural foundation for spin-dependent interatomic potentials and coupled atom-spin dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper presents mHIP-NN, a magnetic extension of HIP-NN that incorporates rotationally invariant spin correlations into hierarchical message-passing layers to enable large-scale simulations of electron-mediated spin dynamics in disordered itinerant magnets, demonstrating accurate reproduction of local torques for Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert dynamics and nonequilibrium spin correlation evolution.
AI.motivation: Conventional exact-diagonalization-based approaches for evaluating effective magnetic forces arising from instantaneous electronic structure in disordered itinerant s-d exchange models are computationally prohibitive for large-scale simulations.
AI.method: mHIP-NN extends HIP-NN by incorporating rotationally invariant spin correlations directly into hierarchical message-passing layers, preserving spin-rotation symmetry while learning emergent magnetic energy landscapes and effective local fields from coupled geometric-spin environments.
AI.result: mHIP-NN accurately reproduces local torques governing Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert dynamics and faithfully captures nonequilibrium evolution of spatial spin correlations following thermal quenches in structurally disordered itinerant s-d exchange models.
AI.conclusion: Symmetry-aware hierarchical message-passing networks provide an efficient and scalable framework for large-scale simulations of frustrated itinerant spin systems and nonequilibrium magnetic dynamics, and the fully differentiable learned energy functional offers a foundation for spin-dependent interatomic potentials and coupled atom-spin dynamics.

title: Local density of states distribution and multifractal eigenvectors of weighted random networks via the cavity approach
summary: We study the local density of states (LDoS) distribution of a general class of weighted Erdős-Rényi graphs. Using the cavity method, we obtain a good approximation to the full LDoS distribution and compact expressions for its power-law tails, which we show to have exponent $3$ in the extended phase. We deduce that the eigenvectors in the continuous part of the spectrum are extended but (weakly) multifractal, and we extract expressions for the associated fractal dimensions and the singularity spectrum. We also demonstrate that the inverse participation ratio in this multifractal phase exhibits an unusual logarithmic scaling with system size, which is neither fully-extended nor localised by the usual definitions. Finally, we verify that some symmetry properties (derived from the non-linear sigma model), which have been shown to hold for many systems exhibiting multifractality, also hold in our case, both for the LDoS distribution and the singularity spectrum.

AI.tldr: The paper uses the cavity method to study the local density of states distribution in weighted Erdős-Rényi graphs, finding power-law tails with exponent 3 in the extended phase, weakly multifractal eigenvectors, logarithmic scaling of the inverse participation ratio, and symmetry properties consistent with the non-linear sigma model.
AI.motivation: To understand the local density of states distribution and multifractal properties of eigenvectors in weighted Erdős-Rényi graphs, a fundamental random graph model, beyond the fully-extended or localised regimes.
AI.method: Cavity method applied to weighted Erdős-Rényi graphs to derive the LDoS distribution, its power-law tails, fractal dimensions, singularity spectrum, and scaling of the inverse participation ratio.
AI.result: LDoS distribution has power-law tails with exponent 3 in the extended phase; eigenvectors are extended but weakly multifractal; the inverse participation ratio shows logarithmic scaling with system size, unusual compared to standard extended/localised phases; symmetry properties from the non-linear sigma model are verified.
AI.conclusion: Weighted Erdős-Rényi graphs exhibit a multifractal phase in the continuous spectrum with distinct logarithmic scaling, and satisfy expected symmetry relations, enriching the understanding of Anderson transitions on random graphs.

title: The UZH protocol: Separating errors and constructing improved CP2K basis sets and pseudopotentials
summary: Reliable density-functional simulations require numerical settings whose residual errors are smaller than the chemical and materials trends being interpreted. In CP2K/Quickstep, this requirement is complicated by the joint use of atom-centered Gaussian basis sets and norm-conserving pseudopotentials: a code-to-code discrepancy usually contains both contributions. We present the UZH protocol, a closed-loop CP2K workflow that calibrates molecularly optimized Gaussian basis sets on small molecules, validates the resulting settings in unary-crystal equation-of-state benchmarks, identifies whether the limiting approximation is the Gaussian basis or the pseudopotential. The diagnosis is then used to revise the parameter files. The central diagnostic is a three-way comparison between production CP2K-GTH-UZH calculations, SIRIUS calculations using the same Goedecker--Teter--Hutter pseudopotential in a systematic plane-wave representation, and all-electron full-potential linearized augmented-plane-wave SIRIUS references. This construction decomposes the practical CP2K error into a Gaussian-basis component and a pseudopotential component. The protocol distinguishes basis-limited noble-gas and heavy-element cases from pseudopotential-limited transition-metal cases, guides targeted revisions with the CP2K basis and pseudopotential optimizers, and produces improved MOLOPT basis sets and GTH pseudopotentials as explicit outputs of the workflow. The UZH protocol is therefore constructive: it does not merely measure or reduce errors a posteriori, but allows turning verification outliers into validated CP2K parameter files for simulations across molecules and condensed phases.

AI.tldr: The UZH protocol is a closed-loop CP2K workflow that calibrates Gaussian basis sets and pseudopotentials by decomposing code-to-code discrepancies into basis and pseudopotential components via three-way comparisons (CP2K-GTH-UZH vs. systematic plane-wave vs. all-electron LAPW), enabling targeted revisions and producing improved MOLOPT basis sets and GTH pseudopotentials for reliable simulations across molecules and condensed phases.
AI.motivation: Reliable DFT simulations require residual errors smaller than the chemical/materials trends being interpreted, but CP2K/Quickstep's joint use of atom-centered Gaussian basis sets and norm-conserving pseudopotentials makes code-to-code discrepancies ambiguous (both contributions entangled). There is no systematic way to identify which approximation (basis or pseudopotential) limits accuracy.
AI.method: Closed-loop CP2K workflow: (1) calibrate molecularly optimized Gaussian basis sets on small molecules, (2) validate in unary-crystal equation-of-state benchmarks, (3) perform three-way comparison between production CP2K-GTH-UZH, plane-wave SIRIUS with same GTH pseudopotential, and all-electron full-potential LAPW SIRIUS references. This decomposes CP2K error into Gaussian-basis component and pseudopotential component.
AI.result: The protocol distinguishes basis-limited (noble-gas, heavy-element) cases from pseudopotential-limited (transition-metal) cases, guides targeted revisions using CP2K's basis and pseudopotential optimizers, and produces improved MOLOPT basis sets and GTH pseudopotentials as explicit outputs.
AI.conclusion: The UZH protocol is constructive: it does not merely measure or reduce errors a posteriori, but allows turning verification outliers into validated CP2K parameter files for simulations across molecules and condensed phases.

title: Electron Paramagnetic Resonance Study of Radical Species on NaNbO3@CeO2-Modified Carbon Vulcan XC72 Gas Diffusion Electrode for Electrochemical Degradation of Paracetamol via Electro-Fenton
summary: While electrochemical oxidation is a promising technology for water treatment, a fundamental understanding of the specific radical mechanisms involved in pharmaceutical degradation has remained limited. This study addresses this gap by employing Electron Paramagnetic Resonance (EPR) spectroscopy to directly quantify the radical species generated during the degradation of paracetamol using a novel gas diffusion electrode (GDE) modified with NaNbO3 nanocubes and CeO2 nanorods. This approach provides a critical advancement beyond prior literature by moving from indirect inference to direct, quantitative analysis of reactive species. Results demonstrated that a boron-doped diamond (BDD) anode (65% OH radical, 35% aryl radicals) drastically outperformed a Platinum (Pt) anode (74% OH radical, 26% aryl radicals), achieving complete degradation in 15 minutes versus 45 minutes and 81.6% versus 67.8% mineralization. Consequently, this work provides a foundational mechanistic framework that fundamentally advances the field, offering not just a more effective material system (BDD/NaNbO3@CeO2-GDE) but also a validated methodology for rationally designing and optimizing electrochemical water treatment processes based on quantifiable radical pathways.

AI.tldr: This study uses EPR spectroscopy to directly quantify radical species during paracetamol degradation, showing BDD anode outperforms Pt anode, and establishes a mechanistic framework for designing electrochemical water treatment processes.
AI.motivation: The fundamental understanding of specific radical mechanisms in electrochemical pharmaceutical degradation has remained limited, as prior work relied on indirect inference rather than direct quantification of reactive species.
AI.method: EPR spectroscopy directly quantified radicals during paracetamol degradation using a novel gas diffusion electrode (GDE) modified with NaNbO3 nanocubes and CeO2 nanorods, comparing boron-doped diamond (BDD) and platinum (Pt) anodes.
AI.result: BDD anode (65% OH radical, 35% aryl radicals) achieved complete degradation in 15 minutes and 81.6% mineralization, versus Pt anode (74% OH radical, 26% aryl radicals) requiring 45 minutes and achieving 67.8% mineralization.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a foundational mechanistic framework and validated methodology for rationally designing and optimizing electrochemical water treatment processes based on quantifiable radical pathways, with the BDD/NaNbO3@CeO2-GDE system being particularly effective.

title: A Physics-Informed B-Spline Framework for Continuous Approximation of Flow Data
summary: Continuous approximations of flow data are useful for downstream analysis, differentiation, and visualization, but purely data-driven reconstructions do not, in general, preserve the governing physics. This limitation becomes particularly important when input data are physically inconsistent, whether due to low-fidelity discretizations or unmodeled discrepancies. In such cases, reconstructed fields may exhibit inaccurate PDE residuals, violated balance laws, or unreliable derived quantities. To address this, we propose a physics-informed B-spline framework that embeds physical constraints directly into the reconstruction process. The method constructs compact, continuously differentiable representations of discrete fields using tensor-product B-splines and determines spline control points by solving an optimization problem balancing data fidelity with residuals of the governing PDEs, alongside initial and boundary conditions. Leveraging exact analytical derivatives of the B-spline basis enables efficient and accurate evaluation of physical residuals without storing full-resolution fields. We refer to this approach as physics-informed multivariate functional approximation (PI-MFA). Numerical studies on the 1D convection-diffusion, 2D coupled Burgers, and 2D incompressible Navier-Stokes equations show PI-MFA reduces PDE residuals and improves global balance-law consistency. Compared with standard and regularized MFA, PI-MFA produces more physically faithful reconstructions and, for physically inconsistent data, lower approximation errors, while offering computational advantages over tested physics-informed neural networks. Overall, PI-MFA preserves the compactness, local support, and exact differentiability of classical spline spaces while producing reliable continuous flow fields for scientific analysis and visualization.

AI.tldr: PI-MFA embeds physics constraints into B-spline reconstruction of flow data, producing physically faithful continuous fields with exact differentiability, reducing PDE residuals and improving balance-law consistency over standard methods.
AI.motivation: Purely data-driven reconstructions of flow data fail to preserve governing physics, especially when input data are physically inconsistent due to low-fidelity discretizations or unmodeled discrepancies, leading to inaccurate PDE residuals, violated balance laws, or unreliable derived quantities.
AI.method: Constructs compact, continuously differentiable representations of discrete fields using tensor-product B-splines, with control points determined by optimizing data fidelity against PDE residuals and initial/boundary conditions; leverages exact analytical derivatives of B-spline basis.
AI.result: On 1D convection-diffusion, 2D coupled Burgers, and 2D incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, PI-MFA reduces PDE residuals, improves global balance-law consistency, and achieves lower approximation errors for physically inconsistent data compared to standard/regularized MFA, with computational advantages over PINNs.
AI.conclusion: PI-MFA preserves compactness, local support, and exact differentiability of classical spline spaces while producing reliable continuous flow fields for scientific analysis and visualization.

title: Exactly solvable non-planar $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ dimer liquids on checkerboard and ruby lattices
summary: We generalize an influential framework for exactly solvable quantum dimer models with dual Ising gauge theory descriptions realizing the $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ topological phase from trivalent to tetravalent parent lattices. The resulting quantum dimer models live on crossed-medial lattices and possess the remarkable feature of having crossed plaquettes, leading to transition graphs with generically intersecting loops. This non-planar structure runs counter to established templates for analytically tractable dimer liquids. As the simplest realization of the construction, we introduce an exactly solvable quantum dimer model on the checkerboard lattice that allows an exact mapping to the toric code, thus providing a particularly direct connection between the latter and Anderson's short range resonating valence bond paradigm. We further show that a corresponding crossed ruby lattice construction, dual to an Ising gauge theory on the kagome lattice, naturally falls within the same framework. More generally, the construction gives rise to a broad class of exactly solvable crossed-medial quantum dimer models and admits natural iteration, generating cascades of solvable $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ topological dimer liquids beyond the standard planar setting. We furthermore extend Kasteleyn methods to the relevant non-planar graphs, enabling controlled wave-function deformations away from the commuting-projector points while retaining efficient evaluation of correlation functions.

AI.tldr: This paper generalizes exactly solvable quantum dimer models with ℤ₂ topological order from trivalent to tetravalent parent lattices, introducing crossed-medial lattice constructions that feature non-planar intersecting loops. The simplest realization is an exactly solvable model on the checkerboard lattice mapped to the toric code, with extensions to crossed ruby lattices and cascades of solvable models. Kasteleyn methods are extended to non-planar graphs for controlled wave-function deformations.
AI.motivation: To generalize the framework of exactly solvable quantum dimer models with ℤ₂ topological order—previously limited to trivalent parent lattices—to tetravalent parent lattices, thereby expanding the class of analytically tractable dimer liquids beyond planar settings.
AI.method: The authors introduce crossed-medial lattice constructions derived from tetravalent parent lattices, featuring crossed plaquettes and non-planar transition graphs. They map the simplest case (checkerboard lattice) to the toric code, and extend the construction to crossed ruby lattices dual to kagome Ising gauge theories. Kasteleyn methods are generalized to handle the non-planar graphs, enabling controlled deformations away from commuting-projector points.
AI.result: An exactly solvable quantum dimer model on the checkerboard lattice is shown to map directly to the toric code. A crossed ruby lattice construction dual to kagome Ising gauge theory also falls within the framework. The construction admits natural iteration, generating cascades of solvable ℤ₂ topological dimer liquids. Kasteleyn methods are extended to non-planar graphs for efficient correlation function evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a broad new class of exactly solvable crossed-medial quantum dimer models with ℤ₂ topological order, bridging Anderson's resonating valence bond idea and the toric code in a particularly direct way, and providing tools to study deformations beyond exactly solvable points.

title: Anatomy of fast current-induced skyrmion motion in synthetic antiferromagnets
summary: The high mobility of current-driven skyrmions in synthetic antiferromagnets (SAFs) is widely explained by the macroscopic suppression of the skyrmion Hall effect through gyrotropic force compensation. This established view, however, overlooks a concurrent and significant reduction in the Gilbert damping parameter α, a key factor in the Thiele equation governing skyrmion velocity. Here, we show that this damping attenuation originates from a reconfigured magnon-electron scattering landscape. Using a microscopic s-d model, we demonstrate that the strong antiferromagnetic interlayer Ruderman-Kittel-Kasuya-Yosida (RKKY) exchange coupling in SAFs increases the magnonic gap of skyrmion collective modes, thereby suppressing the thermal magnon population and, consequently, the magnon-electron scattering rate that dominates damping in metallic ferromagnets. Our work establishes a dual-mechanism framework to fully explain the superior kinetics of SAF skyrmions: the macroscopic topological effect rectifies the motion direction, while the microscopic dissipation mechanism reduces the drag. This synergy enables high-speed and efficient motion, providing a fundamental elucidation of the enhanced mobility reported in recent studies such as the work by Pham et al. [Science 384, 307-312 (2024)].

AI.tldr: The paper reveals a dual-mechanism explaining the high mobility of skyrmions in synthetic antiferromagnets: macroscopic gyrotropic force compensation (suppressing skyrmion Hall effect) and microscopic damping reduction via magnonic gap enlargement from strong RKKY coupling, which suppresses magnon-electron scattering.
AI.motivation: The established view attributes SAF skyrmion high mobility solely to macroscopic suppression of the skyrmion Hall effect via gyrotropic force compensation, overlooking the concurrent reduction in Gilbert damping parameter α—a key factor in skyrmion velocity according to the Thiele equation.
AI.method: Using a microscopic s-d model, the authors analyze the strong antiferromagnetic interlayer RKKY exchange coupling in SAFs and its effect on the magnonic gap of skyrmion collective modes, thermal magnon population, and the magnon-electron scattering rate.
AI.result: Strong RKKY coupling increases the magnonic gap of skyrmion collective modes, which suppresses the thermal magnon population and consequently reduces the magnon-electron scattering rate—the dominant damping mechanism in metallic ferromagnets, thereby lowering the Gilbert damping parameter α.
AI.conclusion: SAF skyrmion mobility enhancement arises from a dual mechanism: macroscopic topological effect (gyrotropic force compensation) rectifies motion direction, and microscopic dissipation mechanism (damping reduction via suppressed magnon-electron scattering) reduces drag, together enabling high-speed, efficient motion.

title: Quantum Otto and Carnot Cycles via Skew Ising Model
summary: We investigate the thermodynamic performance of quantum heat engines and refrigerators based on a two-spin system subject to a skew magnetic field. The working substance is described by an interacting spin model that incorporates both spin--spin coupling and anisotropy induced by a tilted magnetic field. We analyze and compare quantum Carnot and Otto cycles, showing that the Carnot cycle exhibits a universal, entropy-driven behavior with smooth phase boundaries, while the Otto cycle displays a much richer structure governed by the interplay between the energy spectrum and nonequilibrium population differences. In particular, we identify a crossover in both efficiency and coefficient of performance as a function of the interaction strength, which arises from the competition between the interaction energy scale and the magnetic field. We further demonstrate that the skew angle induces state hybridization, modifying both the energy levels and occupation probabilities. Our results highlight that interactions and anisotropy, when properly tuned, can enhance thermodynamic performance, and emphasize the importance of multi-level effects in the design of quantum thermal machines.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes quantum heat engines and refrigerators using a two-spin system in a skewed magnetic field, comparing Carnot and Otto cycles. It finds that Carnot cycles show entropy-driven smooth behavior, while Otto cycles reveal richer structure from energy spectrum and nonequilibrium population differences. A crossover in efficiency and coefficient of performance arises from competition between interaction energy and magnetic field. The skew angle induces state hybridization, modifying energy levels and occupation probabilities, showing that tuned interactions and anisotropy can enhance thermodynamic performance in quantum thermal machines.
AI.motivation: To investigate the thermodynamic performance of quantum heat engines and refrigerators based on a two-spin system with spin-spin coupling and anisotropy from a tilted magnetic field, and to understand how interactions and multi-level effects influence quantum thermal machine design.
AI.method: The authors analyze and compare quantum Carnot and Otto cycles for a two-spin working substance with spin-spin coupling and anisotropy induced by a skewed magnetic field, examining the roles of interaction strength, skew angle, energy spectrum, and nonequilibrium population differences.
AI.result: The Carnot cycle shows universal entropy-driven behavior with smooth phase boundaries, while the Otto cycle exhibits richer structure. A crossover in efficiency and coefficient of performance is identified due to competition between interaction energy and magnetic field. The skew angle induces state hybridization, modifying energy levels and occupation probabilities.
AI.conclusion: Interactions and anisotropy, when properly tuned, can enhance thermodynamic performance, highlighting the importance of multi-level effects in quantum thermal machine design.

title: Fabry-Perot Interference, g-factor Anisotropy, and Gate-Tunable Quantum dot in Chiral Tellurium Nanowires
comment: Main text 25 pages, 6 figures, SI 3 figures
summary: Chiral materials with strong spin-orbit coupling offer a unique platform for exploring the interplay between topology, chirality, and quantum transport yet the quantum coherent regime in elemental tellurium nanostructures remains largely unexplored. Here we demonstrate phase-coherent quasi-ballistic transport, anisotropic Zeeman spectroscopy, and gate-tunable quantum dot formation in hydrothermally grown t-tellurium nanowires. Single nanowire field-effect transistors exhibit p-type transport with hole mobilities rising from approx. 80 cm2 V-1 s-1 at 210 K to approx. 190 cm2 V-1 s-1 at 1 K, consistent with a crossover from phonon-limited to Coulomb scattering dominated regimes near 50 K. Notably, devices segregate into two distinct regimes based on their room temperature two-terminal resistance : low-resistance devices (< 30 kOhm) exhibit Fabry-Perot interference, whereas high resistance devices (> 30 kOhm) display Coulomb-blockade behavior revealing a two-terminal resistance-driven transition between quasi-ballistic and strongly localized transport regimes. Zeeman spectroscopy in in-plane and out-of-plane magnetic fields yields highly anisotropic Lande g-factors (an in-plane gparallel = 1.18 and an out-of-plane gperp = 18.41) and directly resolves a spin-orbit energy gap DeltaSO = 0.864 meV from an avoided crossing. These results establish chiral tellurium nanowires as a versatile platform for gate-defined spin qubits exploiting large, tunable g-factors and for hybrid tellurium-superconductor architectures targeting Majorana zero modes in an elemental vdW system.

AI.tldr: Hydrothermally grown tellurium nanowires exhibit phase-coherent quasi-ballistic transport, highly anisotropic Zeeman splitting (g∥=1.18, g⊥=18.41), a spin-orbit gap ΔSO=0.864 meV, and a resistance-driven transition between Fabry-Pérot interference and Coulomb blockade regimes, establishing them as a platform for spin qubits and Majorana zero modes.
AI.motivation: Chiral materials with strong spin-orbit coupling offer a unique platform for exploring topology, chirality, and quantum transport, yet the quantum coherent regime in elemental tellurium nanostructures remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: Hydrothermal growth of t-tellurium nanowires; single nanowire field-effect transistors; transport measurements with in-plane and out-of-plane magnetic fields; Zeeman spectroscopy to extract g-factors and spin-orbit energy gap.
AI.result: Hole mobilities increase from ~80 cm²/V·s at 210 K to ~190 cm²/V·s at 1 K; two transport regimes (Fabry-Pérot interference for R<30 kΩ, Coulomb blockade for R>30 kΩ); anisotropic g-factors (g∥=1.18, g⊥=18.41); spin-orbit gap ΔSO=0.864 meV.
AI.conclusion: Chiral tellurium nanowires are a versatile platform for gate-defined spin qubits with large tunable g-factors and for hybrid tellurium-superconductor architectures targeting Majorana zero modes.

title: Profiling a Rydberg-Atom Electric Field Sensor for Off-Resonant Detection of Sub-100 MHz RF Signals
summary: We present a Rydberg-Atom electric field sensor optimized to detect signals at sub-100 MHz carrier frequencies. The sensing setup employs a sapphire vapor cell that allows for detection of signals below 100~MHz -- typical vapor cells made of glass or quartz demonstrate strong screening of radio frequency (RF) signals in this frequency regime. Applied signals are detected by observing AC Stark shifts in the atomic vapor energy levels. As a test case for the commercial utility of this receiver, we perform our tests at several carrier frequencies in the Industrial, Scientific, and Medical (ISM) band. At each carrier frequency, we report sensitivity, minimum detectable field, and detectable electric-field dynamic range. We also present a routine for optimizing off-resonant signal detection by tuning experimental parameters such as Rydberg coupler laser detuning and RF local oscillator strength. This Python-based optimization routine, which can be used at any off-resonant carrier frequency, is shared on Github for others to use in their own investigations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a Rydberg-Atom electric field sensor optimized for sub-100 MHz carrier frequencies using a sapphire vapor cell to overcome RF screening, demonstrates performance in the ISM band, and provides a Python-based optimization routine for off-resonant signal detection.
AI.motivation: Standard glass or quartz vapor cells strongly screen RF signals below 100 MHz, limiting the applicability of Rydberg-atom sensors at low carrier frequencies. A sapphire vapor cell is used to mitigate this screening and enable detection in this challenging frequency regime.
AI.method: The sensor detects signals via AC Stark shifts in atomic energy levels. A sapphire vapor cell is employed to reduce RF screening below 100 MHz. A Python-based optimization routine tunes experimental parameters (Rydberg coupler laser detuning, RF local oscillator strength) for off-resonant signal detection.
AI.result: Tests were conducted at multiple ISM band carrier frequencies below 100 MHz. Sensitivity, minimum detectable field, and detectable electric-field dynamic range are reported for each frequency.
AI.conclusion: The sapphire vapor cell enables Rydberg-atom electric field sensing at sub-100 MHz carrier frequencies, with demonstrated utility for commercial ISM band applications. The open-source optimization routine facilitates off-resonant detection at arbitrary carrier frequencies.

title: Quantum-geometric origin of superfluid weight in quasicrystals with critical states
summary: A distinctive feature of many quasiperiodic systems is the presence of critical states that are neither extended nor exponentially localized. We investigate the geometric effect on the superfluid weight in quasiperiodic systems with critical states at zero temperature. We employ both real-space and momentum-space approaches to superfluid weight in quasicrystals, which allows us to separate the conventional and quantum geometric contributions. We find that the superfluid weight is dominated by the geometric contribution in quasiperiodic systems with critical states. This finding reveals a fundamental interplay between superconductivity and critical states in quasicrystals.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how critical states (neither extended nor localized) in quasiperiodic systems enhance the quantum geometric contribution to the superfluid weight at zero temperature, finding that the geometric contribution dominates over the conventional one.
AI.motivation: To understand the geometric effect on superfluid weight in quasiperiodic systems that host critical states, and to reveal the fundamental interplay between superconductivity and critical states in quasicrystals.
AI.method: The authors employ both real-space and momentum-space approaches to compute the superfluid weight in quasicrystals, enabling the separation of conventional and quantum geometric contributions.
AI.result: The superfluid weight in quasiperiodic systems with critical states is dominated by the geometric contribution rather than the conventional one.
AI.conclusion: There is a fundamental interplay between superconductivity and critical states in quasicrystals, where geometry plays a key role in determining the superfluid properties.

title: Confidence, Statistical Evidence and Relative Belief with Applications to a Problem in Particle Physics
summary: Probability theory provides a clear definition of what is meant by evidence in favor, against or none either way, of an event occurring for an unobserved response, via the principle of evidence. This is immediately applicable when carrying out a proper Bayesian analysis. Even without a prior, this imposes restrictions on reported inferences as these need to reflect the likelihood ordering. Relative belief inferences satisfy this requirement and, when the errors in these inferences are controlled, they also satisfy repeated sampling, or frequentist, requirements such as achieving given confidence levels. Relative belief inferences are considered here for the construction of intervals for uncertainty quantification in the context of a Poisson model for a signal with background noise. These intervals are contrasted with the well-known Feldman-Cousins intervals for this problem.

AI.tldr: The paper presents relative belief inferences for constructing uncertainty intervals in a Poisson signal-plus-background model, contrasting them with Feldman-Cousins intervals. Relative belief inferences satisfy both likelihood-based evidential principles and frequentist coverage requirements.
AI.motivation: To develop interval estimates for uncertainty quantification in Poisson signal-with-background models that respect the likelihood ordering principle (evidential reasoning) while also achieving proper frequentist coverage, unlike standard approaches that may sacrifice one for the other.
AI.method: Relative belief inferences are applied to construct intervals for a Poisson model with background noise. The intervals are derived from the relative belief ratio, which respects likelihood ordering. Error control ensures frequentist validity. These intervals are compared to the classical Feldman-Cousins approach.
AI.result: Relative belief intervals satisfy both the evidential (likelihood ordering) and frequentist (repeated sampling coverage) requirements for the Poisson signal-plus-background problem.
AI.conclusion: Relative belief inferences provide a principled framework for uncertainty quantification that unifies Bayesian evidential reasoning with frequentist performance guarantees, specifically demonstrated in the Poisson model with background noise.

title: Limits of Trap-assisted Photomultiplication Gain
summary: Photodiodes based on trap-assisted current injection can exhibit internal photomultiplication with apparent quantum efficiencies far exceeding unity, raising the question of whether such gain fundamentally enhances detector sensitivity. We employ a minimal analytical framework based on a single gain-active trapped state coupling photogenerated carriers to contact injection. The gain is intrinsically self-limiting: the injection process that amplifies the current simultaneously accelerates relaxation of the gain-enabling state, producing an inherently nonlinear, operating-point-dependent response. The form of this nonlinearity is not universal -- once the trap level is generalized to an energetic distribution and recombination is allowed to be bimolecular, the same mechanism yields superlinear, linear, or strongly sublinear responses. A single chord gain is therefore not a meaningful device descriptor, and chord-gain comparisons across the literature conflate devices in different regimes. Treating trap occupancy and injection as coupled stochastic processes, we show that internal gain introduces a strictly non-negative fluctuation penalty from the dissipative dynamics that sustain the gain state. A local, small-signal detectivity exhibits a finite optimum yet cannot exceed the intrinsic thermodynamic limit of the underlying unity-gain photodiode. Gain is thus equivalent to driven stochastic amplification: it can suppress downstream readout noise, but cannot reduce the fundamental noise floor set by the primary photodetection process.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically demonstrates that internal photomultiplication gain in photodiodes is fundamentally self-limiting, creates nonlinear operating-point-dependent responses that cannot be captured by a single gain value, and introduces a non-negative fluctuation penalty that prevents gain from improving the fundamental thermodynamic detectivity limit set by the primary photodetection process.
AI.motivation: To address whether trap-assisted current injection gain in photodiodes can fundamentally enhance detector sensitivity beyond the intrinsic thermodynamic limit of unity-gain photodiodes.
AI.method: A minimal analytical framework based on a single gain-active trapped state coupling photogenerated carriers to contact injection, generalized to an energetic distribution with bimolecular recombination. Coupled stochastic processes analysis of trap occupancy and injection.
AI.result: Gain is intrinsically self-limiting; chord gain is not a meaningful device descriptor; internal gain introduces a strictly non-negative fluctuation penalty; small-signal detectivity has a finite optimum that cannot exceed the intrinsic thermodynamic limit of the underlying unity-gain photodiode.
AI.conclusion: Gain is equivalent to driven stochastic amplification that can suppress downstream readout noise but cannot reduce the fundamental noise floor set by the primary photodetection process.

title: Minimization of disorder as a key design principle for natural sizes of light harvesting 2 complexes
summary: The light harvesting 2 (LH2) complex of purple bacteria has excellent energy conversion efficiency. Clarifying the design principle behind such efficiency at the atomistic level is crucial for understanding its structure-function relationship, and can be utilized for the design of artificial light harvesting systems. To this end, we conducted comprehensive computational investigation of the dynamical and statistical nature of electronic excited states of pigment molecules in a natural LH2 complex with 9-fold symmetry and its two non-natural {\it in silico} analogues with 6- and 12-fold symmetries. To ensure reliable and efficient all-atomistic molecular dynamics simulations, we combined a well established interpolation approach for the construction of the potential energy surface with a neural network machine learning approach. Outcomes of these calculations clarify that non-natural forms of LH2-type complexes have significantly larger quasistatic disorder than those for the natural one. In addition, non-natural systems have more disruptions of the hydrogen bonding, underscoring its crucial role for reducing the disorder. On the other hand, local environmental dynamics are relatively insensitive to the structural changes although there is moderate enhancement in the anharmonic or interatomic components for the synthetic ones. These findings based on all-atomistic simulations provide direct computational evidence that the structure and sizes of natural LH2 complexes are designed to minimize the energetic disorder. We analyze quantitative implications of these for the energy transferring capability of the LH2 complex.

AI.tldr: Using all-atomistic simulations combining interpolation and neural network methods, this study shows that natural LH2 complexes (9-fold symmetry) exhibit lower quasistatic energetic disorder than non-natural analogues (6- and 12-fold symmetry), with hydrogen bonding playing a key role in minimizing disorder, highlighting the structural design principle for efficient energy transfer.
AI.motivation: To clarify the atomistic design principle behind the excellent energy conversion efficiency of the LH2 complex in purple bacteria, and to inform the design of artificial light-harvesting systems.
AI.method: Comprehensive computational investigation using all-atomistic molecular dynamics simulations, combining an interpolation approach for constructing potential energy surfaces with a neural network machine learning approach, comparing natural 9-fold symmetric LH2 with in silico 6- and 12-fold symmetric analogues.
AI.result: Non-natural LH2 analogues exhibit significantly larger quasistatic disorder and more disruption of hydrogen bonding than the natural complex; local environmental dynamics are relatively insensitive to structural changes, though with moderate enhancement in anharmonic/interatomic components for synthetic complexes.
AI.conclusion: Natural LH2 complexes are structurally designed to minimize energetic disorder, with hydrogen bonding playing a critical role; direct computational evidence supports that the structure and sizes of natural LH2 are optimized for efficient energy transfer.

title: Flow-based generative models for amortized Bayesian inference in regression and inverse PDE problems
summary: Bayesian inference provides a principled framework for uncertainty quantification in scientific machine learning. However, conventional Bayesian approaches usually require solving a new inference problem for each observation set, causing substantial computational costs that hinder real-time applications like online monitoring and digital twins. Furthermore, inferring over infinite-dimensional function spaces with varying observation sets poses major challenges for existing amortized inference methods. In this work, we propose Flow-ABI, a flow-based generative framework for amortized Bayesian inference in regression and inverse partial differential equation (PDE) problems. It consists of two components: (i) a functional prior model that learns expressive priors from historical data and physical knowledge through flow matching, and (ii) a set-conditioned functional posterior sampler mapping observation sets to functional posterior distributions. The learned posterior model naturally accommodates varying, permutation-invariant observation sets, and generalizes across different observation discretizations. Once trained, Flow-ABI enables near-real-time posterior sampling for previously unseen observations without retraining or iterative optimization. The proposed methodology can be seamlessly integrated with a wide class of scientific machine learning frameworks, including physics-informed neural networks and neural operators, for uncertainty-aware inverse PDE modeling. Experiments demonstrate that Flow-ABI accurately captures both Gaussian and non-Gaussian posterior distributions while achieving over two-order-of-magnitude speedups relative to the gold-standard Bayesian inference method, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. These results show Flow-ABI is an effective, scalable, and computationally efficient framework for uncertainty quantification in scientific machine learning.

AI.tldr: Flow-ABI is a flow-based generative framework for amortized Bayesian inference in regression and inverse PDE problems. It uses functional prior modeling via flow matching and set-conditioned functional posterior samplers to enable near-real-time posterior sampling from varying, permutation-invariant observation sets without retraining, achieving >100x speedups over Hamiltonian Monte Carlo.
AI.motivation: Conventional Bayesian inference requires solving new inference problems for each observation set, incurring high computational costs that hinder real-time applications like online monitoring and digital twins. Existing amortized inference methods struggle with infinite-dimensional function spaces and varying observation sets.
AI.method: Flow-ABI consists of two components: (i) a functional prior model that learns expressive priors from historical data and physical knowledge via flow matching, and (ii) a set-conditioned functional posterior sampler that maps observation sets to functional posterior distributions, accommodating varying, permutation-invariant observation sets. It integrates with PINNs and neural operators.
AI.result: Flow-ABI accurately captures both Gaussian and non-Gaussian posterior distributions while achieving over two-order-of-magnitude speedups relative to Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, the gold-standard Bayesian inference method.
AI.conclusion: Flow-ABI is an effective, scalable, and computationally efficient framework for uncertainty quantification in scientific machine learning, enabling near-real-time posterior sampling for unseen observations without retraining or iterative optimization.

title: Atomic-scale visualization of the toroidal order in a trimeric Dy(III) single-molecule toroic
summary: Single-molecule toroics (SMTs) offer a unique platform for next-generation quantum devices utilizing head-to-tail spin alignments in the compounds. Presence of toroidal moments in SMTs has been essentially based on magnetometry and ab initio calculations. Here, we report observation and probe of the toroidal moment in [Dy3(OH)(teaH2)3(paa)3]Cl(OMe) [teaH3: triethanolamine; paaH: N-(2-pyridyl)-acetoacetamide] from mapping of Dy3+ magnetic susceptibility tensors by polarized neutron diffraction (PND). Neutron diffraction under variable magnetic fields demonstrates field-induced magnetization along the c-axis with toroidal moments anti-parallelly stacked, providing definite proof of the toroidal moment. Magnetometry studies confirm the toroidal ground state. For the first time, the combined use of PND, variable-field neutron diffraction, ab initio calculations, and magnetometry is introduced as a robust and quantitative methodology to probe molecular-scale toroidal magnetism. This integrated approach overcomes limitations of earlier indirect methods, establishes a benchmark framework for investigating SMTs, and provides valuable insights for the design of molecular quantum materials.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the first direct observation of the toroidal moment in a single-molecule toroic (SMT) [Dy₃(OH)(teaH₂)₃(paa)₃]Cl(OMe) using polarized neutron diffraction (PND), combined with variable-field neutron diffraction, ab initio calculations, and magnetometry, establishing a robust quantitative methodology for probing molecular-scale toroidal magnetism.
AI.motivation: Single-molecule toroics (SMTs) are promising for next-generation quantum devices, but prior evidence for toroidal moments relied solely on indirect methods (magnetometry and ab initio calculations). Direct experimental observation was lacking, motivating the development of a definitive probe.
AI.method: The authors employed polarized neutron diffraction (PND) to map Dy³⁺ magnetic susceptibility tensors, variable-field neutron diffraction to observe field-induced magnetization with anti-parallel toroidal stacking, ab initio calculations, and magnetometry — integrating these techniques for the first time as a comprehensive methodology.
AI.result: Neutron diffraction under variable magnetic fields revealed field-induced magnetization along the c-axis with anti-parallel stacking of toroidal moments, providing definitive proof of the toroidal moment. Magnetometry confirmed the toroidal ground state.
AI.conclusion: The integrated approach overcomes limitations of earlier indirect methods, establishes a benchmark framework for investigating SMTs, and provides valuable insights for designing molecular quantum materials.

title: Dominant in-plane anomalous Hall effect in a monoclinic room-temperature ferromagnet
summary: Ferromagnetic metals are characterized by enhanced dissipationless transverse transport responses via the anomalous Hall effect, offering a route towards magnetic sensing and spintronic readout functionalities. In most ferromagnets, the anomalous Hall current is constrained to lie in the plane perpendicular to the magnetization (or applied magnetic field). Recently, it has been recognized that selected symmetries can also permit a Hall response in a traditionally forbidden configuration, where the Hall current lies in the same plane as the magnetization, realizing an in-plane anomalous Hall effect. Reported realizations of this effect, however, are typically much weaker than the conventional Hall response in the same material. Here, through engineering specific crystallographic mirror symmetry-breaking, we realize a strongly enhanced in-plane anomalous Hall response in monoclinic Cr3Te4 with room-temperature ferromagnetism. Remarkably, the in-plane anomalous Hall signal exceeds the out-of-plane response by a factor of five, with which we demonstrate a unique in-plane field and current sensing functionality. Combined with density functional theory calculations, our results establish low-crystalline-symmetry ferromagnets with near-Fermi-level Weyl points as a practical platform for symmetry-engineered Hall responses, and point to a route towards room-temperature, geometry-flexible sensing devices.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates a strongly enhanced in-plane anomalous Hall effect in monoclinic Cr3Te4, where the in-plane Hall signal exceeds the out-of-plane response by a factor of five, enabled by engineering crystallographic mirror symmetry-breaking, and showcases its application for room-temperature magnetic sensing.
AI.motivation: In-plane anomalous Hall effect (AHE) has been previously realized but is typically much weaker than the conventional out-of-plane AHE. The authors aim to achieve a strongly enhanced in-plane AHE through symmetry engineering.
AI.method: The authors engineer specific crystallographic mirror symmetry-breaking in monoclinic Cr3Te4, a room-temperature ferromagnet, to realize a strongly enhanced in-plane anomalous Hall response. They combine transport measurements with density functional theory calculations to characterize the effect.
AI.result: The in-plane anomalous Hall signal exceeds the out-of-plane response by a factor of five. The effect is demonstrated for in-plane field and current sensing functionality at room temperature.
AI.conclusion: Low-crystalline-symmetry ferromagnets with near-Fermi-level Weyl points serve as a practical platform for symmetry-engineered Hall responses, enabling room-temperature, geometry-flexible sensing devices.

title: Computing phase diagrams using a convex hull algorithm
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy and Astrophysics
summary: We present a simple universal computational algorithm for computing compositional phase diagrams of rocks and their melts at given temperature and pressure. It makes use of the mathematical concept of the convex hull of a set of points in the space spanned by the composition and the Gibbs free energy. All the complexities of determining the stability or separation of phases, the localization and orientation of tie lines, as well as the determination of characteristic points, curves and surfaces such as the solidus, liquidus, solvus, and the eutectic/peritectic points etc, are taken care of by the algorithm that computes the convex hull, supplemented with an algorithm to physically classify the resulting simplices. For the convex hull computation, the publicly available Qhull package can be used, which is available in SciPy. This makes this method accessible and intuitive for a broad set of scientific and educational applications. Although the method is not practical for systems of a large number of components, it is remarkably stable and efficient for systems of up to four. We present our implementation of the method as a publicly available Python package.

AI.tldr: A simple algorithm using convex hull in composition-Gibbs free energy space to compute phase diagrams of rocks and melts, implemented as a public Python package.
AI.motivation: To provide an accessible, intuitive, and universal computational method for determining compositional phase diagrams of rocks and their melts, avoiding the complexities of traditional manual phase analysis.
AI.method: Uses the convex hull of points in composition-Gibbs free energy space (via Qhull/SciPy) to automatically determine phase stability, tie lines, solidus, liquidus, solvus, eutectic/peritectic points, supplemented by a physical classification algorithm for simplices.
AI.result: The algorithm is remarkably stable and efficient for systems of up to four components, though not practical for large component systems.
AI.conclusion: The method democratizes phase diagram computation through a publicly available Python package, making it broadly accessible for scientific and educational use.

title: Higher-winding phases in one-dimensional non-Hermitian topological superconductors
summary: Non-Hermitian topological superconductors provide a setting in which point-gap topology, non-Hermitian skin effects, and Majorana zero modes are strongly intertwined. In this work, we adopt a coefficient-based approach for computing winding numbers and deriving analytical expressions for phase boundaries in one-dimensional non-Hermitian topological superconductors characterized by point-gap topology with $\mathbb{Z}$ invariants. We apply this approach to two non-Hermitian topological superconducting lattice models, with and without sublattice degrees of freedom, including longer-range hoppings, thereby accessing a much broader parameter space. These extensions generate higher-order polynomials and support phases with higher winding numbers, reflecting the underlying $\mathbb{Z}$ topology. We further clarify how a weak perturbation suppresses the non-Hermitian skin effect while preserving the sublattice-symmetry-protected invariant associated with Majorana zero modes. The predicted winding numbers are verified by open-boundary spectra, where one or multiple pairs of zero-energy boundary modes appear consistently with the bulk invariant. We also examine the stability of these modes against onsite disorder through the inverse participation ratio. Our results provide a systematic and efficient route to constructing topological phase diagrams for higher-winding non-Hermitian topological superconductors.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a coefficient-based method to compute winding numbers and phase boundaries in 1D non-Hermitian topological superconductors with point-gap topology, applied to lattice models with extended parameter spaces, revealing higher winding numbers, suppression of the non-Hermitian skin effect under weak perturbations, and verification of Majorana zero modes via open-boundary spectra and disorder analysis.
AI.motivation: To provide a systematic and efficient coefficient-based approach for computing topological invariants and phase boundaries in non-Hermitian topological superconductors, which have complex interplay between point-gap topology, non-Hermitian skin effects, and Majorana zero modes.
AI.method: A coefficient-based approach for computing winding numbers and analytical phase boundaries, applied to two 1D non-Hermitian superconducting lattice models (with/without sublattice degrees of freedom, including longer-range hoppings), with verification via open-boundary spectra and inverse participation ratio analysis.
AI.result: The method accesses broader parameter spaces with higher-order polynomials, revealing phases with higher winding numbers (ℤ topology). Weak perturbations suppress the non-Hermitian skin effect while preserving sublattice-symmetry-protected invariants. Open-boundary spectra show one or multiple pairs of zero-energy modes consistent with bulk invariants. The stability of these modes against disorder is confirmed via inverse participation ratio.
AI.conclusion: The coefficient-based approach offers a systematic and efficient way to construct topological phase diagrams for higher-winding non-Hermitian topological superconductors.

title: Ytterbium lattice clock with uncertainty of $1.1\times 10^{-18}$ and instability of low $10^{-19}$
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures. Submitted to: Metrologia. This is the pre-peer reviewed version of the article
summary: We report an optical lattice clock based on $^{171}$Yb atoms with a total systematic uncertainty of $1.1\times 10^{-18}$. In-vacuum buildup cavity was employed to enhance the lattice light power. Differential frequency measurement between two identical clocks facilitate the evaluation of systematic shifts. Synchronous comparison of the two clocks reached a stability level of $2.7\times 10^{-19}$ in an averaging time of 216,000 s. The magic frequency $ν_{\mathrm{zero}}$ was determined to be 394 798 258.3(1) MHz. Under typical operating conditions, the lattice light shift is controlled at an uncertainty level of $3\times 10^{-19}$. The blackbody radiation (BBR) shield which is placed in vacuum provides a well-characterized BBR environment, enabling an uncertainty contribution of $8.7\times 10^{-19}$ from the BBR Stark shift. Other systematic shifts have also been evaluated. The two clocks will be used for remote frequency comparisons between Shanghai and Wuhan.

AI.tldr: An optical lattice clock based on $^{171}$Yb atoms achieved a total systematic uncertainty of $1.1\times 10^{-18}$, with a stability of $2.7\times 10^{-19}$ at 216,000 s averaging, featuring in-vacuum cavity enhancement, magic frequency determination at 394,798,258.3(1) MHz, and evaluated systematic shifts including lattice light shift ($3\times 10^{-19}$) and BBR Stark shift ($8.7\times 10^{-19}$).
AI.motivation: To develop an ultra-precise optical lattice clock with total systematic uncertainty at the $10^{-18}$ level, enabling future remote frequency comparisons between Shanghai and Wuhan.
AI.method: Employed in-vacuum buildup cavity for lattice light power enhancement; used differential frequency measurement between two identical clocks for systematic shift evaluation; synchronous comparison for stability characterization; determined magic frequency and controlled BBR environment with in-vacuum shield.
AI.result: Total systematic uncertainty: $1.1\times 10^{-18}$; stability: $2.7\times 10^{-19}$ at 216,000 s; magic frequency: 394,798,258.3(1) MHz; lattice light shift uncertainty: $3\times 10^{-19}$; BBR Stark shift uncertainty: $8.7\times 10^{-19}$.
AI.conclusion: The developed Yb optical lattice clock achieves $10^{-18}$-level systematic uncertainty suitable for remote frequency comparisons between Shanghai and Wuhan.

title: Distribution of Majorana modes in the extended-range Kitaev chain
summary: The topological properties of the Kitaev chain model with extended-range interactions are investigated, focusing on cases where the topological winding number is preserved. We assume that the pairing and hopping terms decay algebraically in space with exponents $α$ and $β$, respectively. We show that in the truncated-range scenario, there are as many distinct topological phases as the number of coupled neighboring sites. In addition, an explicit analytical formulation is provided to evaluate the topological invariant and the phase transitions that emerge in these systems. Besides the analytical description, we introduce a new physical insight into the topological excitations of the ground-state by measuring the spatial distribution of the edge modes with the Majorana average position. Taking the next-nearest neighbor Kitaev chains as a probe, various numerical calculations of Majorana edge states were performed in finite-size clusters to determine the sensitivity of the topological zero energy modes to the parameters of interest. The occupation of edge-to-edge non-local fermion states is computed and defined as an effective parity. Such an effective parity exhibits new interesting features beyond the energetic exchange from the ground-state fermion parity switches, which are related to the distribution of the respective edge modes. Our calculations show a direct correlation between the ground-state fermion parity and the edge occupation numbers, which are translated into localization and delocalization of the Majorana average position.

AI.tldr: The paper studies Kitaev chains with extended-range (algebraically decaying) hopping and pairing, showing that the number of topological phases equals the number of coupled neighbors. It provides analytical formulas for topological invariants and phase transitions, and introduces the Majorana average position to probe edge mode spatial distributions. Numerical simulations on next-nearest neighbor chains reveal correlations between ground-state fermion parity, edge occupation, and edge mode localization/delocalization.
AI.motivation: To understand how extended-range (algebraically decaying) interactions affect topological properties of Kitaev chains, and to develop analytical and numerical tools for characterizing topological phases and edge modes in such systems.
AI.method: Analytical formulation of topological invariants and phase transitions for Kitaev chains with algebraically decaying pairing (exponent α) and hopping (exponent β). Numerical simulations on finite-size next-nearest neighbor chains, using Majorana average position to measure edge mode spatial distribution and effective parity to characterize edge-to-edge non-local fermion states.
AI.result: In truncated-range scenarios, the number of distinct topological phases equals the number of coupled neighboring sites. A direct correlation exists between ground-state fermion parity and edge occupation numbers, which translates into localization/delocalization of Majorana average position. The effective parity reveals features beyond energetic ground-state parity switches.
AI.conclusion: Extended-range interactions in Kitaev chains preserve the topological winding number while enriching the phase diagram. The Majorana average position and effective parity provide novel insights into topological excitations and edge mode behavior in these systems.

title: Filamentary Transport and Thermoelectric Effects in Mushroom Phase Change Memory Cells
summary: We performed a 2D finite-element electrothermal computational study of thermoelectric effects and filamentary electronic transport in Ge$_2$Sb$_2$Te$_5$ mushroom phase change memory cells during Reset and Set operations, accounting for spatial activation energy variations in amorphous Ge$_2$Sb$_2$Te$_5$ and phase-change dynamics. Reset operations with current going from the top electrode to the narrow 4 nm bottom electrode require $\sim$3x less energy and power, and $\sim$2x lower current to achieve the same Reset resistance, compared to the opposite polarity, due to thermoelectric effects. Filamentary conduction, electrical breakdown, thermal runaway, and local crystallization of amorphous Ge$_2$Sb$_2$Te$_5$ depend on current polarity and thermal boundary conditions, and determine the location, shape, and volume of the programming region, which may be significantly smaller than the semi-cylindrical mushroom region. The programming volume does not scale with contact dimensions larger than 10 nm. Larger contact areas introduce increased device-to-device and cycle-to-cycle variability due to filamentary conduction but are expected to lead to higher reliability and endurance.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a 2D finite-element electrothermal study of thermoelectric effects and filamentary transport in Ge₂Sb₂Te₅ mushroom phase change memory cells during Reset/Set operations, showing that polarity-dependent thermoelectric effects reduce Reset energy/power by ~3× and current by ~2×, and that filamentary conduction determines the programming region which does not scale beyond 10 nm contact dimensions.
AI.motivation: To understand how thermoelectric effects and filamentary electronic transport influence the programming characteristics (Reset/Set operations) of Ge₂Sb₂Te₅ mushroom phase change memory cells, particularly regarding polarity effects, energy efficiency, and scalability.
AI.method: 2D finite-element electrothermal computational study accounting for spatial activation energy variations in amorphous Ge₂Sb₂Te₅ and phase-change dynamics.
AI.result: (1) Reset operations with current from top to narrow bottom electrode require ~3× less energy/power and ~2× lower current for same Reset resistance. (2) Filamentary conduction, electrical breakdown, thermal runaway, and crystallization depend on current polarity and thermal boundaries. (3) Programming volume can be significantly smaller than the mushroom region and does not scale with contacts >10 nm. (4) Larger contacts increase variability but improve reliability/endurance.
AI.conclusion: Thermoelectric effects strongly influence phase change memory performance and polarity matters significantly; filamentary conduction limits scaling of the programming region beyond 10 nm contacts, introducing a trade-off between variability and reliability.

title: Fe3O4 Nano-octahedra/Vulcan XC72: Optimization and Combination with Solar-Based Electro-Fenton for Progestins Degradation
summary: The widespread presence of synthetic progestins, such as levonorgestrel (LNG) and gestodene (GES), in aquatic environments poses significant ecotoxicological risks due to their endocrine-disrupting properties. In this study, nano-octahedral magnetite (Fe3O4-NO) was synthesized via a hydrothermal route and incorporated into gas diffusion electrodes (GDEs) supported on Vulcan XC72 to enhance the in-situ electrogeneration of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). High-resolution transmission electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, SEM, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and contact angle measurements thoroughly characterized the physicochemical and morphological properties of the materials. The 3% Fe3O4-NO/C catalyst provided a two-fold increase in H2O2 selectivity compared with Vulcan XC72. Electrochemical performance was optimized using a 2^3 factorial design and principal component analysis (PCA), with current density, pH, and Na2SO4 concentration as variables. The optimized GDE (3% Fe3O4-NO/C) achieved a maximum H2O2 production of 0.44 +/- 0.02 g L-1 with a current efficiency of 43.1 +/- 0.23% and a specific energy consumption of 0.012 +/- 0.009 kWh g-1. The electrode was further applied to the degradation of LNG and GES using solar and anodic-assisted electro-Fenton processes. Under optimal conditions, over 70% removal of both progestins was achieved, with stable performance across three operational cycles. These findings demonstrate the potential of 3% Fe3O4-NO/C-GDEs as efficient, reusable cathodes for sustainable electrochemical advanced oxidation processes (EAOPs) in water treatment.

AI.tldr: This study synthesized nano-octahedral magnetite (Fe3O4-NO) on Vulcan XC72 to create 3% Fe3O4-NO/C gas diffusion electrodes, which doubled H2O2 selectivity and achieved efficient degradation of synthetic progestins (levonorgestrel and gestodene) via solar and anodic-assisted electro-Fenton processes, with over 70% removal and stable performance over three cycles.
AI.motivation: Synthetic progestins (LNG, GES) in aquatic environments pose ecotoxicological risks due to endocrine-disrupting properties, motivating the need for efficient, sustainable water treatment technologies.
AI.method: Nano-octahedral magnetite (Fe3O4-NO) was synthesized hydrothermally and incorporated into Vulcan XC72-supported gas diffusion electrodes. Physicochemical characterization used HRTEM, XRD, SEM, XPS, and contact angle measurements. Electrochemical optimization employed a 2^3 factorial design with PCA, and degradation was performed via solar and anodic-assisted electro-Fenton processes.
AI.result: The 3% Fe3O4-NO/C catalyst doubled H2O2 selectivity vs. bare Vulcan XC72. Optimized GDE achieved 0.44 ± 0.02 g L⁻¹ H2O2, 43.1 ± 0.23% current efficiency, and 0.012 ± 0.009 kWh g⁻¹ energy consumption. Over 70% removal of both progestins was achieved with stable performance across three operational cycles.
AI.conclusion: 3% Fe3O4-NO/C-GDEs are efficient, reusable cathodes for sustainable electrochemical advanced oxidation processes (EAOPs) in water treatment, particularly for removing endocrine-disrupting progestins.

title: An adaptive framework for the axisymmetric pulsar magnetosphere using physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold networks
comment: 25 pages, 10 figures. Submitted to Journal of Computational Physics
summary: The pulsar magnetosphere has only recently been addressed using Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), by deploying a domain-decomposition approach and treating the separatrix and equatorial current sheet as infinitesimally thin discontinuities. However, this baseline requires extensive manual hyperparameter tuning, achieves limited final accuracy and demands several hours of training. We refine this framework by introducing domain-specific neural architectures based on Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, an automated adaptive training pipeline and a physics-based convergence criterion that eliminate the need for manual calibration. The proposed methodology delivers self-consistent axisymmetric magnetosphere solutions with mean squared errors of the PDE residuals at O(1e-6) in double precision - an improvement of two orders of magnitude over the baseline - while achieving convergence in under 20 minutes in single precision. Importantly, the method reliably resolves stellar radii reduced by up to 80% compared to the baseline, overcoming the severe spatial scale disparities that also challenge traditional solvers. Furthermore, by varying the flux that opens to infinity, we provide a correction to the equation that connects it to the equatorial T-point's position. The complete framework is released as the open-source library PulsarX.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a refined PINN framework using Kolmogorov-Arnold networks and automated training to solve pulsar magnetosphere problems, achieving two orders of magnitude improvement in accuracy (MSE ~1e-6) and convergence in under 20 minutes, while resolving stellar radii reduced by up to 80% compared to the baseline.
AI.motivation: Existing PINN-based pulsar magnetosphere solvers require extensive manual hyperparameter tuning, achieve limited accuracy, and demand several hours of training. The severe spatial scale disparities challenge both traditional solvers and existing neural approaches.
AI.method: The authors replace standard architectures with domain-specific Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, implement an automated adaptive training pipeline with a physics-based convergence criterion, and deploy the framework in both double and single precision modes.
AI.result: The method achieves mean squared errors of PDE residuals at O(1e-6) in double precision (two orders of magnitude improvement), convergence in under 20 minutes in single precision, and reliably resolves stellar radii reduced by up to 80% compared to baseline. It also provides a corrected equation connecting open flux to the equatorial T-point position.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach significantly outperforms the baseline PINN framework for pulsar magnetosphere modeling, eliminating manual calibration, drastically reducing training time, and improving accuracy. The open-source library PulsarX is released to facilitate further research.

title: Correlation-driven phonon renormalisation and the equation of state of $γ$-cerium
summary: We investigate the thermodynamic properties of elemental cerium by assessing the crucial role of phonon free energy within the framework of dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT). While conventional density functional theory (DFT) often fails to capture the intricate energy landscape of $f$-electron materials, our approach integrates many-body electronic correlations with lattice dynamics to achieve a more rigorous description of the equation of state. We calculate the total energy as a function of the lattice constant at both the DFT and DFT+DMFT levels, subsequently incorporating the vibrational free energy derived from the phonon density of states. Our findings reveal that electronic renormalisation of the force constants significantly alters the phonon spectra, particularly in the strongly correlated $γ$-phase. By applying these phonon corrections to the energy profiles, we observe a substantial refinement in the predicted equilibrium volumes. Using principal-component-based machine learning, we interpolate phonon dispersions continuously from a finite set of first-principles calculations and compare them to experiment, finding significantly closer agreement compared to conventional DFT and DFT+U calculations that neglect dynamical many-body correlations. This study underlines the necessity of accounting for both electronic and vibrational entropy when evaluating the phase stability and structural transitions of lanthanide systems under varying pressures and temperatures.

AI.tldr: This paper integrates dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) with phonon free energy calculations to study elemental cerium, showing that electronic renormalization of force constants significantly alters phonon spectra, especially in the γ-phase, and that incorporating vibrational corrections improves predicted equilibrium volumes beyond conventional DFT and DFT+U methods. Machine learning interpolation of phonon dispersions yields closer agreement with experiment.
AI.motivation: Conventional DFT fails to capture the complex energy landscape of f-electron materials like cerium. The authors aim to achieve a more rigorous description of the equation of state by integrating many-body electronic correlations with lattice dynamics.
AI.method: The total energy is calculated as a function of the lattice constant at both DFT and DFT+DMFT levels. Vibrational free energy from the phonon density of states is incorporated. Principal-component-based machine learning is used to interpolate phonon dispersions from a finite set of first-principles calculations.
AI.result: Electronic renormalization of force constants significantly alters phonon spectra, particularly in the strongly correlated γ-phase. Applying phonon corrections to energy profiles yields substantial refinement in predicted equilibrium volumes. Machine learning interpolated phonon dispersions show significantly closer agreement with experiment compared to conventional DFT and DFT+U calculations.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for both electronic and vibrational entropy is necessary when evaluating phase stability and structural transitions of lanthanide systems under varying pressures and temperatures.

title: Predicting Defect States: A Quick Screening Protocol for Substitutional Point Defect Engineering
summary: Point defects in crystalline materials play a central role in determining electronic, optical, and magnetic properties. However, systematic exploration of defect configurations remains computationally expensive because large supercell calculations are required to approximate isolated defects under periodic boundary conditions. We present a unit-cell-based tight-binding protocol that enables rapid pre-screening of substitutional defects. The protocol extracts Wannier tight-binding Hamiltonians from small, fully relaxed unit cells of the host and defect-like systems, replicates the host Hamiltonian to construct a supercell model, and introduces the defect by modifying only the on-site energies at the substitution site while leaving the hopping parameters unchanged. We validate the protocol across three diverse systems: isostructural substitutional defects in transition-metal dichalcogenides (M$_\mathrm{Mo}$ MoS$_2$, M = Ce, Zr, Nb, Tc, and Ru), symmetry-breaking carbon substitutions in hexagonal boron nitride (C$_\mathrm{B}$C$_\mathrm{N}$ h-BN), and nitrogen-vacancy (NV$^-$) centers in diamond. These case studies span two-dimensional and three-dimensional hosts, simple substitutions, and substitution-vacancy complexes. In all cases, the protocol successfully captures the number of in-gap states, their degeneracies, and their shallow or deep character relative to host band edges, despite some quantitative deviations in absolute energy positions. We further identify limitations for vacancies of highly electronegative atoms and for charge-state or spin-polarization effects, both of which involve self-consistent charge redistribution not captured by the protocol.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a unit-cell-based tight-binding protocol for rapidly pre-screening substitutional point defects in crystalline materials, validated on TMDs, h-BN, and diamond NV- centers, accurately capturing in-gap states and defect character despite limitations in absolute energy positions and treatment of charge/spin effects.
AI.motivation: Systematic exploration of point defect configurations is computationally expensive due to large supercell calculations needed to approximate isolated defects under periodic boundary conditions; a faster pre-screening method is needed.
AI.method: A unit-cell-based tight-binding protocol that extracts Wannier tight-binding Hamiltonians from small relaxed unit cells, replicates the host Hamiltonian to build a supercell, and introduces the defect by modifying only on-site energies at the substitution site while keeping hopping parameters unchanged.
