AI.result: Validated on three systems: isostructural substitutions in MoS2 (M = Ce, Zr, Nb, Tc, Ru), C substitutions in h-BN, and NV- centers in diamond. The protocol successfully captures the number of in-gap states, degeneracies, and shallow/deep character, though with quantitative deviations in absolute energy positions.
AI.conclusion: The protocol enables rapid defect pre-screening but has limitations for vacancies of highly electronegative atoms, charge-state effects, and spin-polarization effects due to the lack of self-consistent charge redistribution.

title: The Two Dimensional Dynamical Bulk Boundary Correspondence: Beyond Two Band Models
summary: A dynamical equivalent of the bulk-boundary correspondence has been suggested to occur in one and two dimensional topological models following sudden quenches. Depending on the topological invariant of the time evolving and initial phases involved large boundary contributions to a dynamical free energy occur. Moreover they occur periodically between the critical times at which this dynamical free energy becomes non-analytic, \emph{i.e.}~at dynamical quantum phase transitions. At these critical times the eigenvalue spectrum of the Loschmidt matrix which underlies the dynamical free energy closes its gap. The boundary contributions are understood to be due to zero-modes or in-gap bands of this matrix, forming a close analogy with equilibrium topological models and their edge modes. The exact cause of this phenomena and its generality remain unknown. In this article we test the dynamical bulk-boundary correspondence for a complicated two dimensional topological superconductor with a rich phase diagram, allowing quenches between many different Chern numbers. We show that there is no straightforward correspondence between the equilibrium phases quenched between and the dynamical bulk boundary correspondence. Furthermore the correspondence can depend on the orientation of the edges, suggesting a possible weak topological variant.

AI.tldr: This paper tests the dynamical bulk-boundary correspondence in 2D topological superconductors after sudden quenches, finding no straightforward relationship between equilibrium topological phases and dynamical boundary contributions; the correspondence is orientation-dependent and may have a weak topological variant.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether the dynamical bulk-boundary correspondence, previously observed in 1D and 2D topological models, holds generally in a complicated 2D topological superconductor with a rich phase diagram, and to understand the exact cause and generality of this phenomenon.
AI.method: Testing the dynamical bulk-boundary correspondence by performing sudden quenches between phases with different Chern numbers in a 2D topological superconductor and analyzing boundary contributions to the dynamical free energy, its non-analyticities at critical times (dynamical quantum phase transitions), and the eigenvalue spectrum of the Loschmidt matrix.
AI.result: No straightforward correspondence exists between the equilibrium phases involved in the quench and the dynamical bulk-boundary correspondence. The correspondence depends on edge orientation, suggesting a possible weak topological variant.
AI.conclusion: The dynamical bulk-boundary correspondence is not universal or simply determined by equilibrium topological invariants; it is more complex and orientation-dependent in higher-dimensional topological systems.

title: Electrical Spectroscopy of Intervalley Relaxation in WSe$_2$ Transistors
summary: We show that the transconductance of multilayer WSe$_2$ field-effect transistors serves as a direct electrical spectrometer of the intervalley relaxation time $τ_{\rm iv}$, previously accessible only by ultrafast optical techniques. Extending an equilibrium valley-thermodynamics framework with a single relaxation equation for the $Γ$-valley carrier fraction $f_Γ(t)$, we predict three signatures: (i)~a Lorentzian transconductance $g_m(ω)=g_{m,0}+g_{m,v}^0/(1+iωτ_{\rm iv})$, whose imaginary part peaks at $ω_c=τ_{\rm iv}^{-1}$ with opposite signs for bilayer and trilayer; (ii)~a two-stage current transient after a gate step, exhibiting bilayer overshoot or trilayer undershoot; and (iii)~sweep-rate-proportional hysteresis whose gate-voltage profile and layer-number sign reversal distinguish valley from trap-induced dynamics. All three signatures provide quantitative electrical access to $τ_{\rm iv}$ with standard rf and dc instrumentation.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that transconductance in multilayer WSe₂ FETs can directly measure intervalley relaxation time (τᵢᵥ) electrically, bypassing ultrafast optical techniques. A valley-thermodynamics model predicts three electrical signatures: (i) Lorentzian transconductance with layer-dependent imaginary peaks, (ii) two-stage current transients with bilayer overshoot/trilayer undershoot, and (iii) sweep-rate-dependent hysteresis with layer-number sign reversal. All signatures enable quantitative τᵢᵥ extraction using standard rf/DC instrumentation.
AI.motivation: Intervalley relaxation time τᵢᵥ in multilayer WSe₂ has previously been accessible only through ultrafast optical techniques, which are complex and not easily integrated with electronic device characterization. The authors aim to develop a purely electrical method to probe this fundamental valley dynamics parameter.
AI.method: The authors extend an equilibrium valley-thermodynamics framework by incorporating a single relaxation equation for the Γ-valley carrier fraction f_Γ(t). They analytically derive transconductance frequency response, transient current behavior, and hysteresis characteristics in multilayer WSe₂ field-effect transistors.
AI.result: Three distinct electrical signatures of intervalley relaxation are predicted: (i) a Lorentzian transconductance g_m(ω) whose imaginary part peaks at ω_c = τᵢᵥ⁻¹ with opposite signs for bilayer vs. trilayer; (ii) two-stage current transients showing overshoot in bilayers and undershoot in trilayers after a gate step; (iii) sweep-rate-proportional hysteresis with gate-voltage profile and layer-number-dependent sign reversal that distinguishes valley dynamics from trap-induced effects.
AI.conclusion: All three predicted signatures provide quantitative electrical access to τᵢᵥ using standard rf and DC instrumentation, eliminating the need for ultrafast optical measurements and enabling practical valleytronics characterization in electronic devices.

title: Quantum study of ultracold atom-ion excitation exchange
summary: The quantum dynamics of ultracold collisions between rubidium atoms and excited metastable strontium ions is treated in the laboratory frame, enlightening the importance of the coupling between internal angular momenta of the particles and their mutual rotation. The study reveals a subtle competition between electronic excitation exchange and fine structure quenching, with no charge exchange, which is found to be very sensitive to the details of ion-atom interactions. The rate constant for electronic excitation exchange is found in agreement with the experimental results of Ben-Shlomi \textit{et al.} (Phys. Rev. A \textbf{102}, 031301(R) (2020)), while the rate for fine structure quenching is predicted to strongly depend on the initial polarization of the reactants.

AI.tldr: This paper studies ultracold collisions between Rb atoms and excited Sr+ ions, revealing competition between electronic excitation exchange and fine structure quenching without charge exchange. The excitation exchange rate matches experiments, while fine structure quenching depends on initial polarization.
AI.motivation: To understand the quantum dynamics of ultracold ion-atom collisions and the role of coupling between internal angular momenta and molecular rotation, particularly the competition between electronic excitation exchange and fine structure quenching.
AI.method: Quantum dynamics treated in the laboratory frame, analyzing couplings between internal angular momenta of particles and mutual rotation.
AI.result: No charge exchange occurs; electronic excitation exchange rate constant agrees with Ben-Shlomi et al. (Phys. Rev. A 102, 031301(R) (2020)); fine structure quenching rate strongly depends on initial polarization.
AI.conclusion: The dynamics reveal a subtle competition between electronic excitation exchange and fine structure quenching that is highly sensitive to ion-atom interaction details.

title: Microscopic Investigation of the Superconducting State in CuCo$_{2}$S$_{4}$: Evidence for an Intermediate-Coupling Fully Gapped Superconductor
summary: The thiospinel compound CuCo$_2$S$_4$ provides an attractive platform for exploring superconductivity in transition-metal chalcogenide spinels. Here, we report the first microscopic investigation of the superconducting state in CuCo$_2$S$_4$ using muon spin rotation and relaxation ($μ$SR) measurements, complemented by magnetization and heat-capacity experiments. The temperature dependence of the superconducting depolarization rate obtained from transverse-field $μ$SR measurements indicates a fully gapped superconducting order parameter. The extracted gap ratio $2Δ(0)/(k_{\mathrm{B}}T_\mathrm{SC}) = 3.95(2)$ exceeds the BCS weak-coupling value of 3.53, placing CuCo$_2$S$_4$ in the intermediate electron-phonon coupling regime. Zero-field $μ$SR measurements were performed to probe possible time-reversal symmetry breaking (TRSB) in the superconducting state. Within the experimental resolution, no additional spontaneous internal magnetic fields are observed below $T_c$. However, due to the presence of a ferromagnetic impurity phase and the associated fast-relaxing signal component, the sensitivity of the present measurements to weak spontaneous fields is reduced. Consequently, while no evidence for TRSB is detected, its existence cannot be definitively ruled out. Overall, our combined thermodynamic and $μ$SR results demonstrate that CuCo$_2$S$_4$ exhibits a fully gapped superconducting state with intermediate coupling strength, consistent with conventional $s$-wave superconductivity in this cobalt-based thiospinel system.

AI.tldr: CuCo₂S₄ is a fully-gapped superconductor with intermediate electron-phonon coupling (gap ratio 3.95) and no definitive evidence of time-reversal symmetry breaking, consistent with conventional s-wave pairing.
AI.motivation: To microscopically investigate the superconducting state of the thiospinel CuCo₂S₄, an attractive platform for exploring superconductivity in transition-metal chalcogenide spinels, which lacks prior microscopic characterization.
AI.method: Muon spin rotation and relaxation (μSR) measurements in transverse-field and zero-field modes, complemented by magnetization and heat-capacity experiments.
AI.result: (1) The superconducting gap is fully gapped; (2) gap ratio 2Δ(0)/(k_B T_SC) = 3.95(2) exceeds the BCS weak-coupling limit, indicating intermediate electron-phonon coupling; (3) zero-field μSR detected no spontaneous internal fields below T_c, but sensitivity is reduced by ferromagnetic impurity phases, so time-reversal symmetry breaking cannot be definitively ruled out.
AI.conclusion: CuCo₂S₄ is a fully-gapped s-wave superconductor with intermediate coupling strength; no clear evidence of time-reversal symmetry breaking was found, though it cannot be fully excluded due to impurity limitations.

title: Fast-Neutron Irradiation Effect in Heteroepitaxial $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ Schottky Diodes Fabricated on Low-Cost Sapphire Substrates
summary: In this work, we investigate the response of Ni/$β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ Schottky barrier diodes fabricated on c-plane sapphire to fast-neutron irradiation up to a fluence of $1\times10^{15}$ n$\cdot$cm$^{-2}$. The LPCVD-grown heteroepitaxial structure consists of an unintentionally doped buffer, an n$^{+}$ contact layer, and an n-type drift layer, with mesa isolation realized by plasma-free Ga-assisted LPCVD etching. Prior to irradiation, the devices exhibit a turn-on voltage of 1.20 V, specific on-resistance of 8.43 m$Ω\cdot$cm$^2$, ideality factor of 1.32, and Schottky barrier height of 1.29 eV. Following irradiation, the devices remain operational, although the forward current decreases, the turn-on voltage increases to 2.40 V, and the barrier height increases to 1.34 eV. Capacitance-voltage measurements reveal a $\sim$50% reduction in net donor concentration, corresponding to a carrier-removal rate of $\sim$105 cm$^{-1}$. Temperature-dependent measurements from 25 to 250 $^\circ$C confirm that thermionic emission remains the dominant transport mechanism and show significant suppression of reverse leakage current after irradiation. The breakdown voltage increases from 101 to 135 V, consistent with neutron-induced donor compensation. TCAD simulations show a more uniform electric-field distribution and reduced field crowding at the Schottky edge after irradiation. These results provide insight into neutron-induced donor compensation in heteroepitaxial $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ and demonstrate the ability of LPCVD-grown $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ Schottky diodes on sapphire to maintain stable operation under high-fluence neutron environments relevant to space and nuclear electronics.

AI.tldr: Ni/β-Ga₂O₃ Schottky barrier diodes on c-plane sapphire are irradiated with fast neutrons up to 1×10¹⁵ n·cm⁻². Post-irradiation, forward current decreases, turn-on voltage rises from 1.20 V to 2.40 V, barrier height increases to 1.34 eV, net donor concentration drops ~50% (carrier-removal rate ~105 cm⁻¹), and breakdown voltage improves from 101 V to 135 V. Devices remain operational with thermionic emission dominant, demonstrating viability for space and nuclear applications.
AI.motivation: To investigate the response of heteroepitaxial β-Ga₂O₃ Schottky barrier diodes on sapphire to high-fluence fast-neutron irradiation, assessing their suitability for radiation-hard electronics in space and nuclear environments.
AI.method: LPCVD-grown heteroepitaxial Ni/β-Ga₂O₃ SBDs on c-plane sapphire (UID buffer, n⁺ contact, n-type drift layer) with mesa isolation via plasma-free Ga-assisted LPCVD etching were characterized pre- and post-fast-neutron irradiation (fluence up to 1×10¹⁵ n·cm⁻²) using I-V, C-V, and temperature-dependent measurements alongside TCAD simulations.
AI.result: Turn-on voltage increased from 1.20 V to 2.40 V; barrier height from 1.29 eV to 1.34 eV; net donor concentration reduced ~50% (carrier-removal rate ~105 cm⁻¹); reverse leakage suppressed; breakdown voltage increased from 101 V to 135 V. TCAD showed improved electric-field uniformity post-irradiation.
AI.conclusion: Neutron-induced donor compensation enhances breakdown voltage while maintaining device operation. LPCVD-grown β-Ga₂O₃ SBDs on sapphire are promising for radiation-hard applications in space and nuclear electronics.

title: Bounding the Null Space: Interval-Based Uncertainty Quantification for Non-Identifiable Groundwater Models
summary: Groundwater models are routinely non-identifiable: sparse subsurface observations leave many combinations of parameters, states, and boundary conditions equally consistent with the available data. Existing uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods address this by exploring a finite set of model realizations, but incomplete exploration can systematically underestimate the true range of admissible solutions. We propose a fundamentally different approach based on Optimization-based Bound Tightening (OBBT), which represents uncertainty directly as intervals and tightens them by extremizing variables over a constraint system encoding physical laws and observations. This yields guaranteed outer bounds on all uncertain variables without sampling, side-stepping the exploration problem entirely. To apply OBBT to groundwater flow, we discretize Darcy's law using a finite-volume scheme and handle the resulting bilinear terms through McCormick relaxations. We show that these relaxations can break the sign coupling between fluxes and head gradients, permitting non-physical rotational flow and failing to provide sufficient information for effective bound tightening. We identify flow sign prescription and irrotationality constraints as effective remedies and characterize their respective strengths and limitations. We demonstrate the framework on three numerical examples - a 1D steady-state model, a 2D steady-state model across four experimental configurations, and a 2D transient model on a hexagonal grid - and discuss computational performance, scalability, and directions for future research. OBBT offers a conservative, deterministic, and physically grounded alternative to ensemble-based UQ, with natural connections to null space theory and data assimilation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Optimization-based Bound Tightening (OBBT) as a deterministic, conservative alternative to ensemble-based uncertainty quantification for non-identifiable groundwater models, addressing the exploration problem by extremizing variables over constraint systems. It handles bilinear terms via McCormick relaxations, identifies sign coupling and irrotationality issues, and demonstrates the framework on 1D and 2D steady-state and transient examples.
AI.motivation: Groundwater models are routinely non-identifiable due to sparse subsurface observations, and existing UQ methods systematically underestimate uncertainty due to incomplete exploration of parameter/state combinations.
AI.method: OBBT represents uncertainty as intervals and tightens bounds by extremizing variables over a constraint system encoding physical laws and observations. Darcy's law is discretized via finite-volume scheme; bilinear terms are handled through McCormick relaxations. Flow sign prescription and irrotationality constraints are introduced to remedy non-physical rotational flow.
AI.result: Demonstrated on 1D steady-state, 2D steady-state (4 configurations), and 2D transient (hexagonal grid) models. McCormick relaxations can break sign coupling between fluxes and head gradients, causing non-physical rotational flow. Sign prescription and irrotationality constraints effectively remedy this.
AI.conclusion: OBBT offers a conservative, deterministic, physically grounded alternative to ensemble-based UQ with natural connections to null space theory and data assimilation. Computational performance, scalability, and future research directions are discussed.

title: Coherent manipulation of Kondo Majoranas in two-channel Kondo setups
summary: We study coherent manipulation of Majorana zero modes emerging in overscreened two-channel Kondo systems. Using compactified lattice models, we show that these interacting Kondo Majoranas support non-local qubits and admit teleportation, fusion, and braiding operations. In particular, we identify a distinction between non-topological and genuinely topological Y-junction geometries, the latter realizing a non-Abelian geometric holonomy. Our results establish a proof-of-principle route toward coherent control of non-Abelian anyons beyond conventional free-fermion platforms.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that Majorana zero modes in overscreened two-channel Kondo systems can support non-local qubits and topological operations (teleportation, fusion, braiding), with a key distinction between non-topological and topological Y-junction geometries that enable non-Abelian geometric holonomy, establishing a route for coherent control of anyons beyond free-fermion platforms.
AI.motivation: To achieve coherent control of non-Abelian anyons in interacting systems beyond conventional free-fermion platforms, specifically by studying Majorana zero modes in overscreened two-channel Kondo systems.
AI.method: Using compactified lattice models to study coherent manipulation of Majorana zero modes in two-channel Kondo systems, analyzing non-local qubits, teleportation, fusion, and braiding operations, with particular focus on distinguishing non-topological vs. topological Y-junction geometries.
AI.result: Identified that these interacting Kondo Majoranas support non-local qubits and admit teleportation, fusion, and braiding operations. Established a crucial distinction between non-topological and genuinely topological Y-junction geometries, where the latter realizes non-Abelian geometric holonomy.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a proof-of-principle route toward coherent control of non-Abelian anyons in interacting Kondo systems, extending beyond the limitations of conventional free-fermion platforms.

title: Synthesis and Characterization of Atomically-Sharp Superconductor-Dielectric Interface
summary: Modification of superconductor-dielectric interfaces is known to strongly impact coherence times of superconducting quantum devices. This relationship is thought to arise from differences in the concentration of "two-level system" defects in the disordered dielectrics and superconductor-dielectric interfaces; these defects couple to electromagnetic modes in the device and cause dissipation. Zirconium oxide barrier layers on niobium have emerged as a promising pathway to low-loss interfaces in recent years, evidently due to the crystalline nature of these layers in comparison to the amorphous niobium native oxide. We explain the unique ability of zirconium oxide to form a crystalline layer, to maintain a sharp interface with metallic niobium, and to prevent niobium oxide re-growth in terms of the chemical properties of ZrO$_2$ and the Nb-Zr-O ternary system. We demonstrate a new method to grow air-stable zirconium oxide layers on niobium with a higher level of crystallinity and a sharper oxide-metal interface than previously shown, and provide the first comprehensive microscopic analysis of ZrO$_2$ capping layer properties. These developments pave the way toward vital performance advances in superconducting quantum devices.

AI.tldr: This paper explains why zirconium oxide (ZrO₂) forms crystalline, sharp interfaces on niobium (Nb) that prevent Nb oxide re-growth, based on the chemical properties of ZrO₂ and the Nb-Zr-O ternary system. It presents a new method for growing air-stable ZrO₂ layers with higher crystallinity and sharper interfaces than prior work, with the first comprehensive microscopic analysis, aiming to reduce two-level system defects and improve coherence times in superconducting quantum devices.
AI.motivation: Superconductor-dielectric interfaces strongly impact coherence times in superconducting quantum devices due to two-level system (TLS) defects in disordered dielectrics and interfaces. Zirconium oxide barrier layers on niobium have shown promise for low-loss interfaces, but the underlying chemical reasons for their effectiveness and a comprehensive microscopic understanding have been lacking.
AI.method: The authors analyze the chemical properties of ZrO₂ and the Nb-Zr-O ternary system to explain ZrO₂'s ability to form a crystalline layer, maintain a sharp interface with Nb, and prevent Nb oxide re-growth. They develop a new growth method for air-stable ZrO₂ layers on Nb and perform the first comprehensive microscopic analysis of ZrO₂ capping layer properties, including crystallinity and interface sharpness.
AI.result: The new method produces ZrO₂ layers with higher crystallinity and a sharper oxide-metal interface than previously demonstrated. The chemical analysis explains why ZrO₂ uniquely forms a crystalline layer and acts as an effective barrier against Nb oxide re-growth.
AI.conclusion: These findings pave the way toward performance advances in superconducting quantum devices by enabling low-loss, crystalline dielectric interfaces that reduce TLS defect concentrations.

title: Dynamical Partition Functions of Stochastic Dynamics via Variational Flows
summary: Nonequilibrium thermodynamics is governed by the dynamical partition function, and its computation in high-dimensional continuous-state dynamics is a longstanding challenge. The Feynman-Kac formalism provides a rigorous representation for generating functions of arbitrary path observables; however, practical evaluation beyond low dimensions or the weak-noise limit is hindered by the curse of dimensionality and the exponentially growing replica demands of trajectory-based methods. Here we develop a mesh-free neural variational framework that realizes the Feynman-Kac theorem with generative flow models, recasting tilted stochastic evolution as a time-dependent optimization problem. This approach enables the direct computation of both finite-time and asymptotic trajectory thermodynamics in a unified manner. The method applies to general observables, enabling the evaluation of work, entropy production, and current fluctuations. We demonstrate the accuracy and scalability of this method in various nonequilibrium systems including high-dimensional cases.

AI.tldr: A mesh-free neural variational framework using generative flow models realizes the Feynman-Kac theorem to compute dynamical partition functions and trajectory thermodynamics in high-dimensional nonequilibrium systems, overcoming the curse of dimensionality and replica demands of traditional methods.
AI.motivation: Computing the dynamical partition function in high-dimensional continuous-state nonequilibrium thermodynamics is a longstanding challenge due to the curse of dimensionality and exponential replica demands of trajectory-based methods.
AI.method: Develops a mesh-free neural variational framework that implements the Feynman-Kac theorem using generative flow models, recasting tilted stochastic evolution as a time-dependent optimization problem.
AI.result: Enables direct computation of both finite-time and asymptotic trajectory thermodynamics for general observables (work, entropy production, current fluctuations), with demonstrated accuracy and scalability in various nonequilibrium systems including high-dimensional cases.
AI.conclusion: The neural variational framework successfully overcomes dimensionality limitations and replica demands, providing a unified and scalable approach to computing trajectory thermodynamics in nonequilibrium systems.

title: Strain-programmable exciton diffusion in moiré heterostructures
summary: Moiré superlattices in van der Waals heterostructures have recently gained significant attention as an intriguing platform for studying correlated electronic systems and exotic excitonic properties. Previous reports, however, focused on creating and modulating moiré heterostructures through interlayer twisting or lattice constant mismatches, limiting controls on symmetry of heterostructures. In this work, we show that strain significantly alters the geometry of moiré superlattices by breaking the C3 rotational symmetry. We realize strain-induced moiré superlattices by intentionally regulating interlayer strain in WSe2-MoSe2 heterostructures, which is manifested by linearly polarized interlayer exciton emission coupled to the strain direction. Furthermore, interlayer exciton diffusion was preferentially guided along the stretched moiré superlattice orientations over a wide spatial range, reflecting the strain-modified moiré potentials. Our work highlights strain tuning as a versatile tool for designing moiré superlattices and programming excitonic transport, which opens pathways for van der Waals logic and information processing devices.

AI.tldr: Strain-induced breaking of C3 rotational symmetry in WSe2-MoSe2 moiré superlattices enables linearly polarized interlayer exciton emission and directed exciton diffusion along stretched moiré orientations, offering a new tuning knob for moiré engineering.
AI.motivation: Previous moiré heterostructure control relied on interlayer twisting or lattice mismatch, which limits the ability to tune structural symmetry. Strain is proposed as an alternative degree of freedom to break C3 symmetry and reshape moiré superlattices.
AI.method: Interlayer strain is intentionally regulated in WSe2-MoSe2 heterostructures. Linearly polarized interlayer exciton emission and spatial exciton diffusion measurements are used to probe the strain-modified moiré potentials and superlattice geometry.
AI.result: Strain breaks C3 rotational symmetry, leading to linearly polarized interlayer exciton emission aligned with the strain direction, and preferentially guides interlayer exciton diffusion along the stretched moiré superlattice orientations over a wide spatial range.
AI.conclusion: Strain tuning is a versatile tool for designing moiré superlattices and programming excitonic transport, enabling potential applications in van der Waals logic and information processing devices.

title: Enhanced nondipole momentum offsets in triple ionization of atoms driven by mid-infrared laser fields
summary: We investigate the dependence on wavelength of nondipole effects in triple ionization of Ne driven by intense infrared and mid-infrared laser pulses using a three-dimensional semiclassical model that fully accounts for nondipole effects and the Coulomb singularity in the electron-core interaction. We find in triple ionization of strongly driven Ne a large positive average momentum offset along the direction of laser propagation, which vanishes in the dipole approximation. This positive momentum offset significantly increases with increasing wavelength of the laser pulse. This increase is present for all triple ionization events as well as for the main direct and delayed pathways of triple ionization. We attribute the increase of the momentum offset to the contribution of the effect of the magnetic field of the laser pulse on the bound electrons. This contribution counterbalances the decrease in the strength of the recollisions with increasing wavelength. We find that 1200 nm is an ideal wavelength for experimentally measuring the momentum offset related to correlated three-electron escape.

AI.tldr: Using a 3D semiclassical model, the authors find that in triple ionization of Ne by intense laser pulses, a positive average momentum offset along the laser propagation direction (a nondipole effect) increases significantly with longer wavelengths (e.g., 1200 nm is ideal for measurement), attributed to the magnetic field effect on bound electrons counterbalancing reduced recollision strength.
AI.motivation: To investigate the wavelength dependence of nondipole effects (momentum offset) in triple ionization of Ne driven by intense IR and mid-IR laser pulses.
AI.method: 3D semiclassical model accounting for nondipole effects and the Coulomb singularity in electron-core interaction.
AI.result: A large positive average momentum offset along laser propagation direction is found, which increases significantly with increasing wavelength for all triple ionization events and for both direct and delayed pathways.
AI.conclusion: The momentum offset increase is attributed to the magnetic field effect on bound electrons, which counterbalances the decreased recollision strength at longer wavelengths; 1200 nm is identified as ideal for experimental observation of correlated three-electron escape.

title: Vortex pinning of Ba$_{0.62}$K$_{0.38}$BiO$_3$ investigated by magneto-optical Kerr-effect and magnetization measurements
summary: Vortex pinning plays a crucial role in determining properties of type-II superconductors. For example, it governs the irreversible magnetic response as well as dissipation caused by vortex motion. Here, we study vortex pinning in the three-dimensional oxide superconductor Ba1-xKxBiO3 using ultra-high-resolution magneto-optical Kerr effect (MOKE) and detailed magnetization measurements. We find that the zero-field MOKE signal in the superconducting state exhibits a pronounced magnetic-history dependence. This behavior closely resembles the remanent magnetization caused by trapped vortices. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the observed evolution of the MOKE signals is well described by Bean's critical-state model for trapped vortices. Our results establish MOKE as a viable optical and mesoscopic probe of vortex pinning in type-II superconductors, providing a new complementary approach to investigate mixed-state phenomena. We also find that the training-field dependence of the MOKE is linear near zero training field, without any anomalies indicative of spontaneous time-reversal-symmetry breaking in an unconventional superconducting state. Our study defines a clear protocol to distinguish vortex-induced MOKE responses from those associated with a time-reversal-symmetry broken superconducting order parameter.

AI.tldr: This paper uses ultra-high-resolution magneto-optical Kerr effect (MOKE) and magnetization measurements to study vortex pinning in Ba1-xKxBiO3, demonstrating that MOKE signals arise from trapped vortices and follow Bean's critical-state model, establishing MOKE as a mesoscopic probe of vortex pinning in type-II superconductors.
AI.motivation: Vortex pinning governs the irreversible magnetic response and dissipation in type-II superconductors, yet there was a need for an optical, mesoscopic probe to investigate vortex pinning and distinguish vortex-induced signals from those arising from time-reversal-symmetry breaking in unconventional superconductors.
AI.method: Ultra-high-resolution magneto-optical Kerr effect (MOKE) and detailed magnetization measurements on the three-dimensional oxide superconductor Ba1-xKxBiO3.
AI.result: The zero-field MOKE signal in the superconducting state shows pronounced magnetic-history dependence resembling remanent magnetization from trapped vortices. The evolution of MOKE signals is well described by Bean's critical-state model. The training-field dependence of MOKE is linear near zero field without anomalies indicative of spontaneous time-reversal-symmetry breaking.
AI.conclusion: MOKE is established as a viable optical and mesoscopic probe of vortex pinning in type-II superconductors, providing a new complementary approach to investigate mixed-state phenomena and a clear protocol to distinguish vortex-induced MOKE responses from those associated with a time-reversal-symmetry broken superconducting order parameter.

title: Virtual-Array Operational Modal Analysis of Rolling Tires Using a Single Tire Cavity Accelerometer
comment: Manuscript-Based on Master's Thesis, Virginia Tech, 2020, http://hdl.handle.net/10919/107874
summary: The dynamics of rolling tires significantly influence the low-frequency (0-500 Hz) structure-borne noise within vehicles. Accurately characterizing these dynamics under realistic operating conditions remains challenging. Current state-of-the-art methods, primarily relying on Laser Doppler Vibrometers (LDV), are complex to implement, time-intensive, and generally limited to smooth tires in laboratory environments due to issues with speckle formation on treaded surfaces. This study introduces an innovative strategy for Operational Modal Analysis (OMA) of a rolling tire using a single wireless Tire Cavity Accelerometer (TCA) together with two optical sensors. The methodology leverages the non-integer ratio between the tire and drum diameters in a test rig to create a virtual sensor array. By utilizing optical sensors to time-stamp the cleat impact (on the drum) precisely and the TCA position (on the tire), the vibration responses from multiple revolutions are clustered according to the TCA's circumferential position at the moment of impact. This effectively synthesizes responses from an array of virtual sensors distributed around the tire circumference using data from a single test run. The clustered signals are conditioned using order tracking to remove periodic components arising from contact patch deformation. Both Frequency Domain Decomposition (FDD) and Covariance-based Stochastic Subspace Identification (SSI-Cov) were employed for modal identification. The SSI-Cov method proved more robust, successfully identifying 11 circumferential modes up to 240 Hz. The proposed approach offers a significantly more efficient, cost-effective method for characterizing rolling tire dynamics, which is readily applicable to treaded tires and adaptable for on-road testing.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a novel Operational Modal Analysis (OMA) method for rolling tires using a single wireless Tire Cavity Accelerometer (TCA) and two optical sensors, creating a virtual sensor array through non-integer tire-to-drum diameter ratios. The method successfully identifies 11 circumferential modes up to 240 Hz via SSI-Cov, offering a more efficient and cost-effective alternative to LDV-based approaches, applicable to treaded tires and on-road testing.
AI.motivation: Current state-of-the-art methods for characterizing rolling tire dynamics, primarily using Laser Doppler Vibrometers (LDV), are complex, time-intensive, and limited to smooth tires in lab environments due to speckle formation on treaded surfaces. There is a need for a more efficient, cost-effective method applicable to realistic operating conditions.
AI.method: The method uses a single wireless Tire Cavity Accelerometer (TCA) with two optical sensors. The non-integer ratio between tire and drum diameters in a test rig creates a virtual sensor array. Optical sensors time-stamp cleat impact and TCA position; vibration responses from multiple revolutions are clustered by TCA's circumferential position at impact, synthesizing responses from virtual sensors. Signals are conditioned using order tracking to remove periodic components from contact patch deformation. Both Frequency Domain Decomposition (FDD) and Covariance-based Stochastic Subspace Identification (SSI-Cov) are used for modal identification.
AI.result: The SSI-Cov method proved more robust than FDD, successfully identifying 11 circumferential modes up to 240 Hz. The approach offers significantly improved efficiency and cost-effectiveness compared to LDV-based methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed OMA strategy using a single TCA with optical sensors provides a practical, efficient, and cost-effective solution for characterizing rolling tire dynamics. It is readily applicable to treaded tires and adaptable for on-road testing, overcoming key limitations of existing LDV-based approaches.

title: Full-State and Reduced-Moment Encodings: A Representation-Level View of Equilibrium Quantum Many-Body Theory
summary: Equilibrium quantum many-body methods differ not only in approximation, but in which information they represent explicitly. We formulate this distinction by fixing an equilibrium specification and viewing every representation as an encoder from admissible states to represented variables. The identity encoder gives a full-state representation, whereas a non-injective encoder gives a reduced representation whose value labels a fiber of compatible states. For a specified task, an exact decoder exists on a state class if and only if the task is constant on the encoder fibers within that class. Variational principles, reconstruction correspondences, functionals, kernels, and closures are different realizations of additional structure used to select, restrict, or approximate the task-relevant content of a fiber when the retained variable alone is insufficient. Static moments and imaginary-time correlation functions are unified as restrictions of a complete equilibrium readout functional to different probe families. Within the same principle, quantum embedding can be viewed as consistency or replacement between global and local descriptions through reduced interface encoders and their conjugate fields.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes quantum many-body methods through encoder-decoder frameworks, unifying representations like moments, Green's functions, and embedding theories under a single information-theoretic principle based on fiber compatibility and task-specific decodability.
AI.motivation: To clarify the conceptual distinction between different equilibrium quantum many-body methods, which differ not only in approximation but in what information they explicitly represent, and to provide a unifying framework for understanding reduced representations, variational principles, and embedding theories.
AI.method: Fixing an equilibrium specification and treating each representation as an encoder from admissible states to represented variables. The identity encoder gives full-state representation; non-injective encoders give reduced representations whose values label fibers of compatible states. Exact decoders exist when tasks are constant on fibers. Variational principles, reconstruction correspondences, functionals, kernels, and closures are realizations of selecting/restricting/approximating task-relevant fiber content.
AI.result: Static moments and imaginary-time correlation functions are unified as restrictions of a complete equilibrium readout functional to different probe families. Quantum embedding is viewed as consistency or replacement between global and local descriptions through reduced interface encoders and their conjugate fields.
AI.conclusion: The encoder-decoder formalism provides a principled unification of seemingly disparate quantum many-body methods, including variational approaches, Green's function methods, and embedding theories, by revealing their common structure of information representation and task-specific decodability.

title: Graphlet Histogram Representation Database of Inorganic Crystals
summary: Machine learning models for materials property prediction increasingly rely on representations learned end-to-end from large density-functional-theory databases, limiting their applicability when only scarce experimental data are available. Domain-knowledge-driven representations precomputed from crystal structures alone offer a data-efficient, interpretable alternative, but existing approaches capture at most composition or bonding connectivity and discard local structural geometry. Here, we present Graphlet-MP, a database of graphlet histogram representations for 149,082 inorganic crystals from the Materials Project (MP). Seventy-nine distributions describe each material over three hierarchical graphlet orders: atomic sites, bonded pairs, and bond-angle triplets, extracted via screened Voronoi tessellation from the crystallographic information file. We provide a complete technical specification of the representation, an Earth Mover's Distance metric for comparing materials in this space, and the full precomputed database. An accompanying open-source codebase enables users to generate graphlet histograms for arbitrary crystal structures, including experimentally determined ones, and to extend the database to new materials or target properties.

AI.tldr: Graphlet-MP is a database of graphlet histogram representations for 149,082 inorganic crystals from the Materials Project, using three hierarchical graphlet orders (atomic sites, bonded pairs, bond-angle triplets) extracted via Voronoi tessellation, offering a domain-knowledge-driven, interpretable alternative to end-to-end learned representations for materials property prediction with scarce experimental data.
AI.motivation: Machine learning models for materials property prediction rely on end-to-end learned representations from large DFT databases, limiting applicability when only scarce experimental data are available. Domain-knowledge-driven representations are data-efficient and interpretable, but existing approaches capture at most composition or bonding connectivity and discard local structural geometry.
AI.method: The authors present Graphlet-MP, a database of graphlet histogram representations for 149,082 inorganic crystals. Seventy-nine distributions describe each material over three hierarchical graphlet orders: atomic sites, bonded pairs, and bond-angle triplets, extracted via screened Voronoi tessellation from crystallographic information files. An Earth Mover's Distance metric is provided for comparing materials, along with an open-source codebase for generating graphlet histograms for arbitrary crystal structures.
AI.result: A database of 149,082 inorganic crystals with graphlet histogram representations, complete technical specification, Earth Mover's Distance metric, and open-source codebase for generating and extending representations.
AI.conclusion: Graphlet-MP provides a data-efficient, interpretable, domain-knowledge-driven representation that captures local structural geometry beyond composition and bonding connectivity, enabling materials property prediction from scarce experimental data and extension to new materials or target properties.

title: Improved selector behavior in ultrathin chromium-doped V$_2$O$_3$ films
summary: Devices based on the negative differential resistance effect in chromium doped V$_2$O$_3$ are considered to be promising as selector elements for use in emerging memory technologies, as well as for neuromorphic applications. It is shown by electrical measurements, that the switching effect is maintained for very thin films down to 5 nm, and even improved properties such as a low leakage current and an abrupt transition are observed. For these thicknesses, the behavior of crystalline and amorphous films becomes very similar; most strikingly, a forming step is required in both. Transmission electron microscopy reveals this to be likely due to a thin amorphous layer that forms at the interface to the TiN electrode. Elemental mapping further shows a complex distribution of the chromium dopants, as well as a diffusion of Ti into the layer from the electrode, which might be responsible for the improved properties.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the negative differential resistance effect in Cr-doped V₂O₃ thin films down to 5 nm thickness, finding maintained switching behavior with improved properties, a required forming step in both crystalline and amorphous films, and attributing the behavior to an interfacial amorphous layer and Ti diffusion from the electrode.
AI.motivation: To explore the scalability and underlying mechanisms of Cr-doped V₂O₃ as selector elements for emerging memory and neuromorphic applications, particularly at very thin film thicknesses relevant for device miniaturization.
AI.method: Electrical measurements of switching properties in thin films down to 5 nm; Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to observe interfacial structures; Elemental mapping to analyze Cr dopant distribution and Ti diffusion from the TiN electrode.
AI.result: Switching effect is maintained at 5 nm thickness with improved properties (low leakage current, abrupt transition). Both crystalline and amorphous films exhibit similar behavior and require a forming step. TEM reveals an amorphous interfacial layer at the TiN electrode, and elemental mapping shows complex Cr distribution and Ti diffusion into the film.
AI.conclusion: The improved switching properties in ultra-thin Cr-doped V₂O₃ films are likely due to interfacial phenomena including an amorphous layer formation and Ti diffusion from the electrode, which may be beneficial for selector device performance.

title: Pressure-Driven Structural Phase Competition and Functional Response in Layered LiInP2S6
summary: Understanding how hydrostatic pressure modifies interlayer interactions and competing ionic configurations is essential for controlling the emergent functional properties of layered quantum materials. Here, using first-principles density-functional theory calculations, we investigate the pressure-dependent structural, mechanical, electronic, and optical properties of three competing LiInP2S6 polymorphs: the monoclinic C2/c phase and the trigonal P-31c phase in both in-layer and in-gap configurations. Our results reveal a pressure-induced structural phase transition from the monoclinic ground-state C2/c phase to a trigonal P-31c in-layer phase at ~0.38 GPa, driven by enhanced interlayer coupling and anisotropic lattice compression. In contrast, the trigonal P-31c in-gap phase remains energetically unfavorable due to its stronger interlayer ionic interactions and reduced compressibility. All phases remain mechanically stable under compression (0-26 GPa) and exhibit enhanced mechanical rigidity, elastic wave velocities, and Debye temperatures with increasing pressure. Remarkably, the electronic and optical properties within each phase remain highly robust under pressure, with only moderate changes in the band gap and optical absorption edge (UV-Visible range) under pressure; however, substantial modifications emerge across the pressure-induced structural phase transition. These findings establish LiInP2S6 as a pressure sensitive ionic-vdW material in which subtle changes in interlayer interactions govern structural stability and functional properties.

AI.tldr: First-principles study of LiInP2S6 polymorphs reveals a pressure-induced structural phase transition from monoclinic C2/c to trigonal P-31c in-layer phase at ~0.38 GPa, driven by enhanced interlayer coupling, while electronic/optical properties remain robust within each phase but change significantly across the phase transition.
AI.motivation: Understanding how hydrostatic pressure modifies interlayer interactions and competing ionic configurations is essential for controlling the emergent functional properties of layered quantum materials.
AI.method: First-principles density-functional theory (DFT) calculations investigating pressure-dependent structural, mechanical, electronic, and optical properties of three competing LiInP2S6 polymorphs (monoclinic C2/c, trigonal P-31c in-layer, trigonal P-31c in-gap).
AI.result: Pressure-induced structural phase transition from monoclinic C2/c to trigonal P-31c in-layer phase at ~0.38 GPa; all phases mechanically stable up to 26 GPa; enhanced mechanical rigidity, elastic wave velocities, and Debye temperatures with pressure; electronic/optical properties robust within each phase but substantially modified across the phase transition.
AI.conclusion: LiInP2S6 is a pressure-sensitive ionic-vdW material where subtle changes in interlayer interactions govern structural stability and functional properties.

title: Continuous and discontinuous transitions in the Ising-Heisenberg model on the extended Lieb lattice in a magnetic field
comment: 22 pages, 8 figures, submission to SciPost Physics Core journal
summary: The spin-1/2 Ising-Heisenberg model on the extended Lieb lattice in a magnetic field is exactly mapped onto an effective spin-1/2 Ising model on the square lattice. The ground-state phase diagram comprises the quantum antiferromagnetic (QAF), quantum monomer-dimer (MD), classical ferrimagnetic (FRI), and classical ferromagnetic phase. The MD-FRI ground-state phase boundary extends to finite temperatures as a dome-shaped surface of discontinuous thermal transitions bounded by a line of Ising critical points. The QAF phase is enclosed by a surface of continuous thermal transitions evolving from the QAF-MD and QAF-FRI ground-state phase boundaries. Monte Carlo simulations fully confirm the existence and nature of both continuous and discontinuous thermal phase transitions obtained by exact and approximate analytical calculations.

AI.tldr: A spin-1/2 Ising-Heisenberg model on the extended Lieb lattice is mapped to an effective Ising model on a square lattice. The ground-state phase diagram includes QAF, MD, FRI, and ferromagnetic phases. Thermal phase transitions: MD-FRI boundary yields discontinuous transitions (dome-shaped) bounded by Ising critical points; QAF phase has continuous transitions. Monte Carlo simulations confirm analytical predictions.
AI.motivation: To study the interplay of quantum and classical magnetic interactions on a geometrically frustrated extended Lieb lattice, and to exactly map the mixed-spin model onto a simpler effective Ising model to analytically and numerically characterize its ground-state and thermal phase diagram.
AI.method: Exact mapping of the spin-1/2 Ising-Heisenberg model on the extended Lieb lattice onto an effective spin-1/2 Ising model on the square lattice; combined with exact analytical calculations, approximate analytical methods, and Monte Carlo simulations to determine phase boundaries and transition orders.
AI.result: Ground-state phase diagram contains four phases: quantum antiferromagnetic (QAF), quantum monomer-dimer (MD), classical ferrimagnetic (FRI), and classical ferromagnetic phase. The MD-FRI boundary forms a dome-shaped surface of discontinuous transitions bounded by Ising critical points. The QAF phase is enclosed by a surface of continuous thermal transitions. Monte Carlo simulations confirm the nature of all transitions.
AI.conclusion: The exact mapping approach combined with analytical and numerical methods successfully captures the complete phase diagram, demonstrating both continuous and discontinuous thermal phase transitions in the Ising-Heisenberg model on the extended Lieb lattice.

title: Spin polarisation signatures of Fractionally Charged Skyrmions in Fractional Quantum Hall states
summary:
We investigate spin polarisation and low-energy excitations in fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states using cavity-polariton spectroscopy of high-mobility GaAs quantum wells. By measuring the optical coupling strength of interband Landau-level excitations over the range $1/3 \le ν\le 1$, we extract the spin polarisation of the electron system as a function of filling factor.
  Complete suppression of the oscillator strength of the lowest energy excitation, characteristic of singlet trion formation in fully polarised systems, is reported for the first time in this regime.
  At large magnetic fields, fully polarised FQH states exhibit symmetric depolarisation away from their quantised fillings, analogous to Skyrmionic behaviour near $ν=1$. The depolarisation follows an empirical law $S=ν^*$, where $S$ is the number of spin flips per added magnetic flux quantum and $ν^*$ the effective Composite Fermion filling factor. We interpret this behaviour as evidence for Minimal Fractionally Charged Skyrmions (MFCS) formed from bound spin-flip and quasiparticle excitations.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates spin polarization in fractional quantum Hall states using cavity-polariton spectroscopy in GaAs quantum wells. It reports complete suppression of oscillator strength in the lowest energy excitation at fully polarized states, and observes symmetric depolarization away from quantized fillings that follows S=ν*—interpreted as evidence for Minimal Fractionally Charged Skyrmions (MFCS).
AI.motivation: To investigate spin polarization and low-energy excitations in fractional quantum Hall states, using a novel cavity-polariton spectroscopy approach on high-mobility GaAs quantum wells.
AI.method: Cavity-polariton spectroscopy measuring interband Landau-level excitation coupling strengths over filling factors 1/3 ≤ ν ≤ 1, extracting spin polarization as a function of filling factor.
AI.result: First report of complete suppression of oscillator strength in the lowest energy excitation (characteristic of singlet trion formation in fully polarized systems) in the FQH regime. Observation of symmetric depolarization away from quantized fillings in fully polarized FQH states at high magnetic fields, following the empirical law S=ν*.
AI.conclusion: The depolarization behavior is interpreted as evidence for Minimal Fractionally Charged Skyrmions (MFCS), formed from bound spin-flip and quasiparticle excitations.

title: Colloquium: Nuclear clocks
summary: The Th-229 nuclear isomeric state has the lowest energy of all known nuclear excited states, placing it within the reach of current table-top laser technology. This extraordinary property has made this nuclear isomer an attractive candidate for a nuclear optical clock of incredibly high precision and accuracy, both as isolated trapped Th-229 ions and embedded into solid-state platforms. Activity around Th-229 has surged in recent years, driven by breakthroughs in its direct laser excitation. The underlying nuclear physics that gives rise to this unique isomer will be elucidated, as well as the nearly half-century of efforts that led to its direct excitation. The design and systematics of a Th-229 nuclear clock will be discussed, both in ion traps and in the solid-state. These systematics, such as frequency shifts and quenching channels, can be leveraged both to probe the local chemical environment, and as a control knob during clock operation. Finally, the nuclear clock's high sensitivity to the variations of fundamental constants will be discussed.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews the Th-229 nuclear isomeric state, its direct laser excitation breakthrough, the design and systematics of a nuclear optical clock (in both ion traps and solid-state platforms), and its high sensitivity to variations of fundamental constants.
AI.motivation: The Th-229 isomer has the lowest known nuclear excited-state energy, making it accessible to table-top lasers and enabling a nuclear optical clock with potentially unprecedented precision and accuracy. The paper aims to elucidate the underlying nuclear physics, the historical efforts leading to direct excitation, and the clock's potential for probing fundamental physics.
AI.method: The paper reviews the nuclear physics of the Th-229 isomer, the nearly 50-year path to its direct laser excitation, and the design/systematics of nuclear clocks in both trapped-ion and solid-state platforms. It discusses frequency shifts, quenching channels, and control mechanisms for clock operation.
AI.result: Direct laser excitation of the Th-229 nuclear isomer has been achieved. The clock systematics (frequency shifts, quenching channels) can be used to probe the local chemical environment and as control knobs during operation. The nuclear clock exhibits high sensitivity to variations of fundamental constants.
AI.conclusion: The Th-229 nuclear isomer is a promising candidate for a nuclear optical clock with ultra-high precision. Its systematics offer both environmental sensing capabilities and operational control, while its sensitivity to fundamental constant variations enables tests of fundamental physics.

title: Superheating field of clean superconductors near the type-I--type-II boundary: the low-temperature Meissner stability limit of niobium
summary: We calculate the low-temperature superheating field $B_{\rm sh}$ of clean superconductors near the boundary between type-I and type-II superconductivity, with particular emphasis on Nb. The calculation is based on the self-consistent nonlinear nonlocal Eilenberger theory and the linear stability analysis of the Meissner state. For a Nb-like material with $κ_{\rm GL}=0.7$, we obtain $B_{\rm sh}\simeq 290\,{\rm mT}$ at $T/T_c=0.2$, using $B_{c0}\simeq 200\,{\rm mT}$. This value is substantially higher than the value obtained by naively extrapolating the Ginzburg--Landau result near $T_c$ to $T\ll T_c$. For a TESLA-shaped Nb accelerator cavity, it corresponds to an intrinsic Meissner-stability limit of about $67\,{\rm MV/m}$.

AI.tldr: The paper calculates the low-temperature superheating field of clean superconductors near the type-I/type-II boundary using Eilenberger theory, finding B_sh ≈ 290 mT for Nb (κ_GL=0.7) at T/T_c=0.2, corresponding to a 67 MV/m intrinsic limit for TESLA-shaped Nb cavities — significantly higher than extrapolated Ginzburg-Landau results.
AI.motivation: To accurately determine the superheating field of clean superconductors like Nb at low temperatures, which is crucial for understanding the ultimate performance limits of superconducting radio-frequency (SRF) cavities, particularly for accelerator applications.
AI.method: Self-consistent nonlinear nonlocal Eilenberger theory combined with linear stability analysis of the Meissner state.
AI.result: For Nb-like material with κ_GL=0.7, B_sh ≈ 290 mT at T/T_c=0.2 (using B_c0 ≈ 200 mT), which is substantially higher than the naively extrapolated Ginzburg-Landau result near T_c.
AI.conclusion: The intrinsic Meissner-stability limit for a TESLA-shaped Nb accelerator cavity is about 67 MV/m, providing a more accurate upper bound for SRF cavity performance at low temperatures.

title: Finite-temperature Fe K-edge X-ray absorption simulations reveal local structural dynamics of an iron(II) photosensitizer in solution and the crystalline phase
summary: Interpreting metal K-edge spectra of flexible photosensitizers requires a structural model that separates electronic signatures from thermal motion, solvent disorder, and crystal-packing effects. We combine Fe K-edge X-ray absorption measurements with second-generation Car--Parrinello ab initio molecular dynamics and all-electron Gaussian and augmented-plane-wave simulations for an iron(II) N-heterocyclic carbene photosensitizer in acetonitrile solution and in the crystalline phase. Ensemble-averaged spectra reproduce the main near-edge features in both environments and preserve the experimentally observed similarity of the first Fe coordination shell upon dissolution. Comparison with radial distributions extracted from extended fine-structure measurements validates the Fe--N and Fe--C coordination shells sampled by the trajectories, while element-resolved pair distributions explain why higher-shell experimental contrast is rapidly lost. The same dynamical ensembles reveal a broad out-of-plane distribution of the terpyridine nitrogen atom and a nearly octahedral distribution of the Fe-centered coordination planes. The results show that finite-temperature X-ray absorption simulations can provide a compact structural-dynamics picture of molecular transition metal photosensitizers by linking local spectra, solvent-phase ligand motion, and medium-range structural disorder within one trajectory-based description.

AI.tldr: Combining Fe K-edge X-ray absorption with ab initio molecular dynamics simulations reveals how thermal motion and solvation affect the electronic structure of an iron(II) NHC photosensitizer, showing that ensemble-averaged spectra capture near-edge features and validate coordination shells.
AI.motivation: Interpreting metal K-edge spectra of flexible photosensitizers requires a structural model that separates electronic signatures from thermal motion, solvent disorder, and crystal-packing effects.
AI.method: Fe K-edge X-ray absorption measurements combined with second-generation Car-Parrinello ab initio molecular dynamics and all-electron Gaussian and augmented-plane-wave simulations for an iron(II) N-heterocyclic carbene photosensitizer in acetonitrile solution and crystalline phase.
AI.result: Ensemble-averaged spectra reproduce main near-edge features in both environments and preserve the experimentally observed similarity of the first Fe coordination shell upon dissolution. Validation of Fe–N and Fe–C coordination shells via EXAFS radial distributions.
AI.conclusion: Finite-temperature X-ray absorption simulations can provide a compact structural-dynamics picture of molecular transition metal photosensitizers by linking local spectra, solvent-phase ligand motion, and medium-range structural disorder within one trajectory-based description.

title: Antiferromagnetic order and magnetic polarons in lightly doped Li$_x$CoO$_2$ (x $\sim$ 0.9)
summary: We investigate the magnetic properties of Li$_x$CoO$_2$ (x$\sim$0.9) using bulk magnetization, specific heat, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy measurements. The dc magnetization, specific heat and NMR measurements, which probe the macroscopic response, indeed show that this compound partially undergoes an antiferromagnetic transition below $T_N \sim$ 10 K. In addition, we observed a weak ferromagnetic response, which gives rise to the history dependence in magnetization measurements at low fields and is observed at temperatures above room temperature. We propose that there are ferromagnetic clusters at high temperatures due to the formation of magnetic polarons out of doped holes. In EPR measurements performed at the $X$-band frequency, only a fraction of the total spins contribute and show Curie-like paramagnetic behavior as reflected in the temperature dependence of the EPR intensity. The temperature variation of the EPR spectra can be understood in the framework of the diffusion of magnetic polarons.

AI.tldr: LiₓCoO₂ (x~0.9) exhibits partial antiferromagnetic transition below 10 K, weak ferromagnetism above room temperature from magnetic polarons, and EPR spectra explained by polaron diffusion.
AI.motivation: To investigate the magnetic properties of LiₓCoO₂ (x~0.9), which is relevant for understanding its behavior as a cathode material and the role of doped holes in magnetic ordering.
AI.method: Bulk magnetization, specific heat, NMR, and EPR spectroscopy measurements were performed to probe both macroscopic and microscopic magnetic responses.
AI.result: Partial antiferromagnetic transition occurs below TN ~ 10 K. Weak ferromagnetic response appears above room temperature due to magnetic polarons formed by doped holes. EPR shows Curie-like paramagnetic behavior from a fraction of spins, with temperature variation explained by magnetic polaron diffusion.
AI.conclusion: LiₓCoO₂ (x~0.9) hosts magnetic polarons at high temperatures leading to weak ferromagnetism, while the majority of the system undergoes antiferromagnetic ordering at low temperatures.

title: Thermodynamic Approach to Momentum Transport in Dense Fluids
summary: We present a new framework for extending Chapman-Enskog theory beyond the hard-sphere fluid model. Rather than relying on effective hard sphere diameters, the approach makes use of on an exchange function which can be related to the thermodynamic properties of the system. We show that two existing extensions, including modified Enskog theory (MET), fit into this new framework. Based on our approach, we propose an alternative to MET that takes into account the potential interaction energy associated with the inter-particle interactions in the fluid. The proposed expression is applied to predicting the shear viscosity of several different simulated fluid models across a wide set of densities $0.05 \leq ρ^* \leq 0.8$ and temperatures $1.5 \leq T^* \leq 4.0$ in Lennard-Jones units. The fluid models considered include both the Weeks-Chandler-Anderson (WCA) fluid and the Lennard-Jones (LJ) fluid. At low and intermediate density, here taken to be $ρ^* \leq 0.3$, we report mean relative prediction errors between $2\%$ and $4\%$ for both these. Across all densities considered, the largest mean relative errors reported are $4.4\%$ and $8.1\%$ for the WCA fluid and LJ fluid respectively. We also investigate other interaction models, including a diatomic molecular model, in order to better understand the limitations of our approach.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a new framework extending Chapman-Enskog theory beyond hard-sphere fluids using an exchange function linked to thermodynamic properties. It proposes an alternative to modified Enskog theory (MET) incorporating potential interaction energy, achieving low prediction errors (2-8.1%) for shear viscosity across WCA and LJ fluids over a range of densities and temperatures.
AI.motivation: To extend Chapman-Enskog theory beyond the hard-sphere fluid model without relying on effective hard sphere diameters, providing a more physically grounded approach for predicting transport properties of realistic fluids.
AI.method: The method introduces an exchange function related to thermodynamic properties, subsumes existing extensions like MET, and proposes a new alternative that incorporates potential interaction energy associated with inter-particle interactions. The approach is validated against simulated fluid models (WCA, LJ, diatomic) across densities 0.05 ≤ ρ* ≤ 0.8 and temperatures 1.5 ≤ T* ≤ 4.0.
AI.result: Mean relative prediction errors for shear viscosity are 2-4% at low/intermediate density (ρ* ≤ 0.3) for both WCA and LJ fluids. Across all densities, largest mean relative errors are 4.4% (WCA) and 8.1% (LJ). Limitations are investigated using diatomic molecular models.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework offers a viable alternative to MET that accounts for potential interaction energy, achieving good accuracy across a wide range of densities and temperatures for multiple fluid models, with identified limitations for more complex molecular systems.

title: Interplay between Aharonov-Bohm and Altshuler-Aronov-Spivak oscillations in phase-pure GaAs/InAs core/shell nanowires of different lengths
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, 12 pages supplemental material including 12
summary: In GaAs/InAs core/shell nanowires, comprising a tubular conducting shell, interference phenomena observed under an axial field and originating from closed-loop states encircling the insulating core, provide an ideal platform for superconducting quantum devices that utilize effects such as Aharonov--Bohm or Altshuler--Aronov--Spivak-type conductance oscillations. Both effects are different in nature with respect to phase rigidity because of interference of non-time-reversed or time-reversed paths, respectively. Since their occurrence is largely governed by averaging effects, which depend on sample dimensions and the transport regime, we present a systematic study of flux-periodic oscillations of phase-pure zinc-blende GaAs/InAs core/shell nanowires as a function of gate voltage for samples with different contact separation lengths. Our analysis shows that with increasing contact separation length, averaging effects result in gradual reduction of $h/e$-periodic Aharonov--Bohm-type oscillations, while the $h/2e$-periodic Altshuler--Aronov--Spivak oscillations and its $h/4e$-periodic higher harmonics are enhanced. The additional phase rigidity seen in the $h/3e$-periodic oscillations is attributed to phase rigidity propagating from the neighbouring lower harmonics. Our tight-binding transport simulations on nanowires of different lengths which contain only a few scattering centers confirm the experimental observations regarding the different harmonics and their phase rigidity. Together, our experimental and simulation findings indicate quasi-ballistic transport with persistent Aharonov--Bohm-, and phase-rigid Altshuler--Aronov--Spivak-type oscillations despite few scattering centers.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically studies flux-periodic conductance oscillations in GaAs/InAs core/shell nanowires, showing that as contact separation increases, $h/e$-periodic Aharonov-Bohm oscillations decrease while $h/2e$-periodic Altshuler-Aronov-Spivak oscillations and higher harmonics are enhanced, with $h/3e$-periodic oscillations attributed to phase rigidity propagation from lower harmonics. Experimental and tight-binding simulation results indicate quasi-ballistic transport with persistent AB and phase-rigid AAS oscillations despite few scattering centers.
AI.motivation: To systematically understand how averaging effects governed by sample dimensions and transport regime influence the coexistence and interplay of Aharonov-Bohm and Altshuler-Aronov-Spivak-type conductance oscillations in GaAs/InAs core/shell nanowires, providing an ideal platform for superconducting quantum devices.
AI.method: Systematic experimental study of flux-periodic oscillations in phase-pure zinc-blende GaAs/InAs core/shell nanowires as a function of gate voltage for samples with different contact separation lengths, complemented by tight-binding transport simulations on nanowires of different lengths containing few scattering centers.
AI.result: Increasing contact separation length causes gradual reduction of $h/e$-periodic AB-type oscillations while enhancing $h/2e$-periodic AAS oscillations and its $h/4e$-periodic higher harmonics. $h/3e$-periodic oscillations arise from phase rigidity propagating from neighboring lower harmonics. Simulations confirm experimental observations regarding different harmonics and their phase rigidity.
AI.conclusion: The findings indicate quasi-ballistic transport with persistent Aharonov-Bohm and phase-rigid Altshuler-Aronov-Spivak-type oscillations despite few scattering centers, demonstrating the robustness of these interference phenomena in core/shell nanowire systems.

title: Dichotomous electronic system in a bilayer Ni$^{1+}$ nickelate
summary: ``Infinite layer'' nickelates (ILNs) ${\cal R}$NiO$_2$ (${\cal R}$=rare earth elements), having empty apical O sites, become superconducting upon hole doping. They display a secondary electron Fermi surface (FS), giving hole doping, arising not from atomic orbitals but from a band based on interstitial density. Newly reported La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_5$F, formally Ni$^{1+}$, provides an unexpected example of ILN with essentially ideal two dimensional character. A partially occupied single band $E^*$, based on interstitial density, has distinct properties, as its strongly anisotropic shape extends over the three ``apical'' layers and leads to a cylindrical electron FS giving self-doping. This interstitial density is associated with a {\it network of valence bands}, including a Ni $d_{xz},d_{yz}$ pair that partners with $E^*$ to provide an incipient non-analytic Dirac point, leading to an unusual type of interstitial density--$d$ band coupling. The $E^*$ electron band and the conventional Ni $dpσ$ band will display a dichotomy of hole and electron quasiparticle behavior in normal state transport and far-IR properties, and likely resulting in unconventional superconducting state properties even for nickelates.

AI.tldr: La₃Ni₂O₅F is a quasi-ideal 2D infinite-layer nickelate superconductor where an interstitial-density-driven cylindrical electron Fermi surface (E*) coexists with conventional Ni bands, producing a Dirac-like coupling and a dichotomy of hole/electron quasiparticle behavior that likely leads to unconventional superconductivity.
AI.motivation: To understand the electronic structure and superconducting mechanism of infinite-layer nickelates, focusing on the role of interstitial density-derived bands (E*) that provide self-doping and unconventional band coupling, using the newly discovered La₃Ni₂O₅F as an ideal model system.
AI.method: Band structure analysis of La₃Ni₂O₅F, focusing on interstitial-density-based E* band that extends over three apical layers, its strongly anisotropic cylindrical Fermi surface, and its coupling with Ni d_{xz},d_{yz} orbitals leading to an incipient non-analytic Dirac point.
AI.result: La₃Ni₂O₅F is an ideal 2D ILN with a single partially occupied E* band of interstitial origin forming a cylindrical electron FS; the E* band partners with a Ni d_{xz},d_{yz} pair to create an incipient non-analytic Dirac point; a dichotomy exists between E* electron band and conventional Ni dpσ hole band in transport and far-IR properties.
AI.conclusion: The interstitial-density-induced electronic structure with the E*-d band coupling and hole/electron dichotomy is key to understanding unconventional superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelates, and La₃Ni₂O₅F provides a clean platform to study these effects.

title: Efficient analytic continuation approach to Bethe-Salpeter excitation spectra in selected energy windows
summary: We explore the merits of building the Bethe-Salpeter absorption spectrum in a specific energy range using analytic continuation techniques. Specifically, we calculate iteratively a few $\bar{\bar α}(z_k)$ polarizability tensors for a coarse set of $(z_k)$ frequencies in the complex-plane. These data allow constructing a continued-fraction representation for $\bar{\barα}(z)$ that is used to calculate the absorption spectrum close to the real energy axis in the desired energy range. The number and location of these sampling complex frequencies are discussed. The importance of building a continued-fraction representation of the full polarizability tensor with matrix-valued coefficients is emphasized. We show how to extract the poles of the continued fraction as a tool for analyzing the resulting spectra. We study as examples the valence excitations of a paradigmatic dipeptide, the C$_{60}$ fullerene and its PCBM derivative, together with the description of the surface plasmon resonance of the Ag$_{20}$ silver cluster. Further, the high-energy C$_{60}$ X-ray absorption spectrum is explored.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using analytic continuation (continued-fraction representation) to efficiently compute Bethe-Salpeter absorption spectra in targeted energy ranges, demonstrating the method on various molecular and nanoscale systems including dipeptides, fullerenes, PCBM, and silver clusters.
AI.motivation: To overcome the computational cost of computing Bethe-Salpeter absorption spectra across broad energy ranges by developing a more efficient method that focuses on specific energy regions using complex-plane analytic continuation.
AI.method: The method computes a few polarizability tensors  α̃̃(z_k) at coarse complex frequencies, constructs a continued-fraction representation with matrix-valued coefficients, and uses this representation to obtain the absorption spectrum near the real axis. The poles of the continued fraction are extracted for spectral analysis.
AI.result: Successfully demonstrated on valence excitations of a dipeptide, C60 fullerene and its PCBM derivative, surface plasmon resonance of Ag20 silver cluster, and high-energy X-ray absorption spectrum of C60.
AI.conclusion: The analytic continuation approach with continued-fraction representation is an effective tool for targeted Bethe-Salpeter spectrum calculations, enabling efficient computation in desired energy ranges with controllable accuracy.

title: Interaction-driven dynamics in graphene flakes as a benchmark for quantum simulation
summary: We study interaction-driven ultrafast dynamics in finite graphene flakes following an optical pump quench in an interacting tight-binding model. By comparing exact real-time evolution with simulations restricted to particle-hole excitation subspaces, we assess when relaxation can be captured by low-order many-body processes and when this is not sufficient. The single-particle orbital entropy provides a compact diagnostic for dynamic correlation growth. For the systems studied here, periodic graphene flakes are well described by low-order excitations, whereas confined geometries require substantial higher-order contributions even for relatively small interaction strengths. The quench protocol combines simple initial-state preparation with strongly correlated dynamics, identifying a promising benchmark problem for future quantum-computing simulations.

AI.tldr: The paper studies ultrafast dynamics in graphene flakes after an optical pump quench, comparing exact simulations with low-order approximations. It finds periodic flakes are well-described by low-order excitations, while confined geometries need higher-order processes. Single-particle orbital entropy is used as a diagnostic for correlation growth.
AI.motivation: To understand when relaxation dynamics in finite graphene systems can be captured by low-order many-body processes versus requiring higher-order contributions, and to identify a benchmark problem for future quantum-computing simulations.
AI.method: Comparing exact real-time evolution with simulations restricted to particle-hole excitation subspaces in an interacting tight-binding model, using single-particle orbital entropy as a diagnostic for dynamic correlation growth.
AI.result: Periodic graphene flakes are well described by low-order excitations, while confined geometries require substantial higher-order contributions even for relatively small interaction strengths.
AI.conclusion: The quench protocol combines simple initial-state preparation with strongly correlated dynamics, serving as a promising benchmark problem for future quantum-computing simulations.
